title: CoinDCX confirms $16 million loss from retired wallets days after CEO called breach reports a 'false alarm'
text: Indian crypto exchange CoinDCX admitted it lost 15.99 million USDT, or roughly $16 million, to an attack targeting deposit wallets it had stopped using after a 2025 hack. The disclosure comes just days after the exchange's co-founder and CEO, Sumit Gupta, told users on X that reports of a breach sounded like "a false alarm." In an update posted to its blog early Sunday, CoinDCX said it noticed unusual activity on Tuesday that "had impacted our old, deprecated wallet infrastructure which had unknown vulnerabilities." The exchange said its automated sweeping service, which moves funds between the exchange's wallets, "had failed for a particular period," so user deposits had built up at an address the exchange no longer used. "This led to a loss of 15.99 million USDT which was absorbed by the company," CoinDCX said. "We want to reiterate that all user funds remain safe in secure, segregated cold wallets, protected by multi-layer custody and offline security controls," CoinDCX wrote, also noting that the exchange's ordinary trades, deposits, and withdrawals continued as usual despite the breach. Admission follows Wednesday's denials Suspicious outflows from CoinDCX wallets were first flagged at 1:30 a.m. ET on Wednesday by Darcy, the co-founder of asset rescue service provider FlashRescue, who posted that roughly 15.99 million USDT and 5,783.81 TRX left CoinDCX's hot wallet and a handful of deposit addresses at 11:35 a.m. ET on Tuesday. All of the funds went to one Tron address. The biggest single transfer was 15,819,002 USDT, and from there the funds were split up and routed to deposit addresses at Binance, OKX and Gate, per Darcy. Gupta replied to Darcy's post less than three hours later. "Thanks for highlighting but this is incorrect and CoinDCX wallets are not breached," he wrote, adding that the addresses in question had been compromised in July 2025 and that "the hackers seem to be re-using the old wallet addresses and this sounds like a false alarm." CoinDCX's own account followed suit four minutes later, calling the claims "misleading" and saying the addresses "have not been used by CoinDCX since" the July 2025 incident. Onchain analyst ZachXBT soon pushed back on CoinDCX's denials. One deposit address, he wrote, "was in use by a [liquidity provider] for 10 months after your July 2025 incident" and that address swept user deposits to CoinDCX's current hot wallet as recently as April and May 2026. "Meaning $15.8M in user deposits was unaccounted for by your team," he wrote. Gupta answered ZachXBT at 5:59 a.m. ET, saying the team was "investigating it further" and that "no user funds will be at loss." By 7:47 a.m. ET, CoinDCX had posted that its sweeping process failed "for a particular period" and that this "led to some operational losses, which were absorbed by CoinDCX." That post didn't put a number on the losses. ZachXBT then advised users to "withdraw all funds from CoinDCX if you value your assets." He wrote that the exchange's co-founders "publicly and privately denied a theft of its assets occurred meaning they straight up lied or are negligently incompetent," though he said he had still helped freeze stolen crypto worth six figures on behalf of the exchange. $16M loss adds to prior incidents The July 2025 hack cost CoinDCX about $44 million, which Gupta blamed at the time on a server breach. Bengaluru police later said hackers posing as recruiters had tricked a CoinDCX software engineer into installing malware on a company laptop that let the hackers access the exchange's internal systems. Onchain drains and phishing attacks aren't the only issues that CoinDCX has faced. Indian police arrested Gupta and co-founder Neeraj Khandelwal in March over a fraud complaint, which CoinDCX said stemmed from scammers impersonating it through a copycat site. Coinbase invested in CoinDCX in October 2025 in a deal Gupta said valued the exchange at $2.45 billion, deepening the U.S.-listed exchange's push into India and the Middle East. Asked about Gupta's earlier statements and ZachXBT's claims, a representative for CoinDCX's public relations agency referred The Block to the company's blog post and did not address specific follow-up questions.

title: Crypto Today: Musk AI warning, China blockchain buildout, Ethereum Hoodi delay
text:
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, Elon Musk warned that more than 200 AI cloud providers face failure or consolidation as financing tightens, raising concerns for Bitcoin miners expanding into AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, China set a 2030 target for completing its national blockchain network and Ethereum developers delayed the Glamsterdam upgrade on the Hoodi testnet after researchers identified potential smart contract security risks.
Elon Musk warns that over 200 specialist AI cloud providers could fail or consolidate as lenders tighten up their purse strings.
Musk said Sunday on X that lenders had largely stopped providing financing to companies without substantial revenue streams outside AI data centers. He said SpaceX had secured $40 billion in debt financing for GPUs because of its investment-grade status and revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket businesses.
“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many,” he said.
Musk’s warning follows an October forecast from research firm Gartner that more than 80% of neocloud providers will cease operating independently by 2030, as the industry struggles to generate sufficient returns on massive AI infrastructure investments.
The warnings could also have implications for Bitcoin miners that have pivoted into AI infrastructure. For example, IREN has expanded into AI cloud services, renting computing power to customers, while Core Scientific provides data center hosting for neocloud customers such as CoreWeave.
China has set a 2030 target for largely completing a national blockchain network under a five-year digital development plan published Friday.
The 15th Five-Year Plan for National Informatization, which sets priorities calls for deeper blockchain use in trade and finance in the Yangtze River Delta, and deployment at scale in manufacturing and agriculture in the Chengdu–Chongqing region in southwestern China.
Friday’s plan was issued by the Central Cyberspace Affairs Commission, a senior body within the ruling Communist Party that coordinates digital development policy.
The document makes the completion target explicit for a project already included in China’s national development plan released in March. A joint policy from the Communist Party’s central leadership and State Council published on Oct. 9 called for its construction.
Ethereum developers have postponed the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet after researchers identified gas-related security risks that could affect how existing smart contracts handle failed transactions.
The Ethereum Foundation (EF) said that the upgrade, originally scheduled for Oct. 26, would be delayed to allow developers to investigate how some proposals interact with smart contracts deployed on Ethereum.
On Oct. 13, Blockchain security firm ChainSecurity warned that two proposals included in Glamsterdam, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, could weaken safeguards against a type of attack called insufficient gas griefing.
The postponement raises uncertainty over Glamsterdam’s mainnet timeline. Ethereum developers had been considering early December, with plans to finalize a schedule following successful Hoodi testing.

title: Over 11 million BTC can't be linked to any known owner
text:
Bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 is no longer a fringe asset but one with growing acceptance on Wall Street. Yet those tracking blockchain data still can't link most BTC to a known owner.
About 11.1 million BTC, roughly 55% of the supply, was classified as unattributed in Galaxy’s October snapshot. Those coins could belong to individuals, institutions the firm hasn’t identified or holders who can no longer access them.
Galaxy’s head of research, Alex Thorn, sees the figure as evidence that self-custody remains widespread, with people keeping control of their bitcoin keys despite the growth of exchanges, funds and institutional custodians.
"More than half of all BTC supply is sitting in addresses with no known attribution despite all the institutionalization and centralized ownership over the years, still a ton of bitcoin (maybe even most) is held by individuals in self-custody," Thorn wrote on X.
Self-custody means holding your own bitcoin keys rather than leaving coins with an exchange or a fund.
Xapo Bank, a bitcoin-focused bank, replied to Thorn's post, saying that large number of coins held in unnamed wallets is a sign that retail investors have been here for over a decade. Bitcoin is often seen as the first market that grew from the bottom up: Retail investors began trading, and institutions then embraced it.
"And why bitcoin is for the people and people 'can be their own bank' Retail have been here for over a decade. Everyone else still catching up," the bank wrote.
BTC is the native token of the Bitcoin blockchain, a public ledger that lets anyone, anywhere, send and receive money. Miners verify these transactions and add them to the ledger, earning newly issued BTC as a reward. The setup is often held up as an example a perfectly competitive market.
A bitcoin address is like a bank account number on bitcoin's public ledger. Anyone can see how many coins sit at an address, while hiding the identity of the owner. Research firms like Galaxy try to put names to addresses by tracking wallets known to belong to exchanges, funds and other big holders.
The entire unnamed 55% stack doesn't necessarily belong to individuals holding their own coins for the long term.
It could include coins that are likely lost, sitting in wallets whose owners have forgotten their keys or have passed away.
Some were mined in bitcoin's early years by miners other than the one behind the Patoshi pattern, a set of bitcoin's earliest mined blocks that researchers link to a single miner, bitcoin's anonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto.
Some could belong to institutions Galaxy hasn't identified, such as funds, companies and OTC desks, which are brokers that arrange large bitcoin trades privately, away from exchanges. Some coins could belong to custody setups that spread coins across many addresses, making them harder to trace.
The other 45% does have names attached, and some of them are big names, including exchanges, ETFs led by BlackRock, the U.S. government and the single biggest holder, "Satoshi Nakamoto (Patoshi Pattern)," at 1,123,658 BTC. Galaxy counts those coins separately, as "the Satoshi-era miner pattern."
Still, for all the ETF headlines, the largest slice of bitcoin is the one nobody can name.

title: Wells Fargo, Cisco, Intuit Among 6 More Companies Objecting to Tokenized Stocks - Decrypt
text:
The list of companies that don’t want their shares traded on OKX and ICE’s planned tokenized stock venue keeps growing.
Wells Fargo, Cisco Systems, and Marvell Technology are among six new issuers named in an updated public notice from OKXICE TSV dated Friday. Arm Holdings, Moderna and Intuit round out the new additions. That brings the total to 22 objecting companies, up from 16 on Oct. 19 and nine on Oct. 15.
Earlier objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Verizon, Broadcom, and UnitedHealth Group. None of the notices explain the companies’ reasons, or what effect an objection has on whether a stock can trade on the platform.
Wells Fargo joins Goldman Sachs as the second major U.S. bank on the list. Arm, Cisco, and Marvell add more chip and networking heavyweights to a roster already crowded with tech names, including Microsoft, Broadcom and Qualcomm.
OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX’s U.S. holding company, plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7. Trades would run through Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC.
The venue is set to operate under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate. Since its Oct. 19 notice, the venue has said it can list shares tokenized by issuers themselves as well as by outside parties, a path none of the objectors appear to have taken yet.
The latest notice spells out the venue’s risks in detail. Beyond pausing when the underlying stock is halted, it doesn’t use circuit breakers. It has no policies addressing maximal extractable value, the profit traders can capture by reordering transactions on a blockchain.
It warns that broker-dealers trading there face unsettled questions about trade reporting and best execution, which could limit their participation and thin out liquidity. Administrators can also upgrade the smart contracts without advance notice to users, and the contract that controls who can trade has been audited only internally.
OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before unveiling the venue this month. Nasdaq, which won SEC approval for its own tokenized securities pilot, has said it will opt its shares out of the exemption. The IMF recently found real demand for tokenized stocks, especially during off hours when the stock market is closed, but warned that the market remains volatile and illiquid.

title: Musk Warns of Mass AI Neocloud Failures Amid Funding Crunch
text:
The warning comes as Gartner forecasts that more than 80% of specialist cloud providers will cease operating independently by 2030.
Elon Musk warns that over 200 specialist AI cloud providers could fail or consolidate as lenders tighten up their purse strings.
Musk said Sunday on X that lenders had largely stopped providing financing to companies without substantial revenue streams outside AI data centers. He said SpaceX had secured $40 billion in debt financing for GPUs because of its investment-grade status and revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket businesses.
“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many,” he said.
A neocloud is a specialist cloud company that rents out computing power for AI, usually through data centers packed with powerful GPUs.
Musk’s warning follows an October forecast from research firm Gartner that more than 80% of neocloud providers will cease operating independently by 2030, as the industry struggles to generate sufficient returns on massive AI infrastructure investments.
The warnings could also have implications for Bitcoin miners that have pivoted into AI infrastructure. For example, IREN has expanded into AI cloud services, renting computing power to customers, while Core Scientific provides data center hosting for neocloud customers such as CoreWeave.
Related: Bitcoin hashrate hits seven-month high as AI shift fails to ease mining competition
In its forecast, Gartner said AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on infrastructure in 2026 and another $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030, but said there is insufficient revenue to deliver profitable returns on all those investments.
The pressure could be particularly acute for neoclouds, which must earn enough from AI computing services to sustain their operations. Larger cloud companies have more diversified revenue streams that could support AI investment for years, Gartner said.
Even strong market growth may not be enough. Gartner forecasts spending on AI-optimized infrastructure-as-a-service will rise from $66 billion in 2027 to $174 billion in 2030, but said most providers could struggle to recover their investment before the current generation of AI chips is replaced.
Musk’s comments came days after SpaceX reported that its “Super Intelligence” business generated $7.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 830% from a year earlier and accounting for more than half of the company’s $14.6 billion in quarterly sales.
The company attributed the growth to new cloud services agreements, its acquisition of Cursor and increased adoption of its Grok AI model.

title: Keystone customers say breach exposed data the hardware wallet maker promised to delete
text: Hardware wallet maker Keystone said a third party obtained customer shipping information from its Shopify-powered online store, exposing sensitive customer information including names, contact details, shipping addresses and order details, such as the items purchased and their prices. In an X post at 1:59 p.m. ET on Saturday, Keystone said it had detected unauthorized access to its official website on Oct. 20. Three days later, "after verifying API activity with Shopify," which powers its online store, the company confirmed that an unidentified third party had obtained sensitive customer information. "You trusted us with those details, and we're sorry we didn't keep them safe," Keystone wrote. Keystone said financial information such as the customers' payment cards and bank details, and sensitive cryptographic information like recovery phrases, private keys and wallet passwords were not exposed in the breach. "We've blocked access, fixed the vulnerability, opened an investigation, and are emailing affected customers," the company said. Keystone did not say how many customers were affected, how the attacker got in, and whether they've exchanged communications with or identified the attacker. The firm has told users on X who asked about the scope of the breach that it is "still conducting a thorough investigation." Keystone said a detailed report will follow in the coming days. Keystone warned that scammers may pose as the company by phone, text, email or mail, offering refunds, replacement devices or "fixes" for orders and addresses. It told customers never to enter a recovery phrase into a device they did not order, and not to follow links sent in messages supposedly from Keystone. Keystone pledged to delete information 180 days after purchase Keystone in the past pitched its data retention policy as a selling point. On Jan. 5, the day Ledger customers were notified of a similar data leak at that wallet manufacturer's e-commerce partner Global-e, Keystone posted on X: "180 days after your order, your shipping data is permanently deleted." In a March post, the company wrote, "Other hardware wallets keep your data forever. We delete your shipping info in 180 days max." Other posts in August reinforce the same message. The company's Privacy Promise page says that "all shipping information is automatically deleted 180 days after your order is placed." Keystone's privacy policy, last updated in May 2021, words the rule differently: it says Keystone erases "all order information of each customer who has not made an order within the last 180 days." A help center article about deletion requests clarifies that "records of the customer's city and country will not be deleted," and that "the final deletion process is handled by Shopify." Customers claim data from older orders was still exposed Several customers have said on X that their data was exposed anyway. "I bought it over two years ago. I received an email notification," @trintaetres_33 wrote on Saturday. Another user, @BlockchainBarmy, said 214 days had passed between their last order and the breach. @PEPE_Whale69 even raised the alarm about a possible breach before Keystone did. In a post on Friday evening, the user said a caller spoofing a Montreal police number had tried to social-engineer them, at one point asking whether Amazon, eBay or Keystone "meant anything" to them. The X user said the caller had details perfectly matching a Keystone order they placed in 2024, well before the claimed 180-day deletion period. Keystone's X account replied at 1:08 a.m. ET on Saturday that it had "initiated an urgent investigation into this matter." The company says it confirmed the breach on Oct. 23. The Block could not verify the users' claims, and Keystone has not publicly responded to questions about whether it followed the 180-day policy. The Block has reached out to the X users with requests for more information. A recent wave of hardware wallet breaches Keystone is the latest hardware wallet maker to disclose a customer data leak this year. In August, Trezor said a breach at its shipping partner ShipMonk exposed personal data of nearly 14,000 customers. The company later said the breach affected about 67,000 more U.S. customers, and that ShipMonk had given written assurances the data was deleted when it had not been. Days after Trezor's first disclosure, SafePal said a flaw in its order-tracking system exposed personal information of nearly 40,000 customers. Earlier this month, Ledger confirmed that devices sold by reseller CryptoBilis contained hardware implants that capture recovery phrases during setup, and onchain researchers estimated losses at more than $86 million. The Block has reached out to Keystone for comment.

title: CoinDCX absorbs $16 million loss from internal process failure tied to retired wallet
text:
CoinDCX, India’s largest crypto exchange by trading volumes, says it has absorbed a $16 million loss after an internal process failed to move customer deposits out of a retired wallet.
It all started last week, when blockchain sleuths flagged about $16 million in suspicious outflows from wallets linked to the Mumbai-based exchange. CoinDCX was quick to dismiss the reports, with CEO Sumit Gupta calling it a false alarm on X.
A spokesperson told CoinDesk that the addresses cited by the sleuths were old ones, created in January 2025 and compromised in the July 2025 hack, which cost the exchange about $44 million, and that CoinDCX had not used them since. In essence, the exchange said the activity did not have any connection with CoinDCX.
But ZachXBT, a well-known on-chain investigator, said at least one of those addresses, labeled TQKJQ, was in use by a liquidity provider and swept user deposits to CoinDCX’s current public hot wallet as recently as April and May 2026.
On Sunday, CoinDCX published a blog post on the activity tied to TQKJQ, saying the wallet belongs to its old operational wallet infrastructure and that the loss was tied to it.
“This wallet belongs to our old operational wallet infrastructure, which was compromised during the security incident we reported on July 19, 2025, and was deprecated as a result,” CoinDCX said.
The post explained that some users mistakenly continued to deposit funds into the deprecated, or retired, addresses even after the exchange deprecated them following the 2025 hack. CoinDCX credited those users’ portfolios the moment the funds reached the deprecated wallet.
A secondary service, which the exchange calls sweeping, was meant to then move the funds from the deprecated address into the primary CoinDCX wallet.
However, that process failed for a particular period, causing deposits to accumulate in the deprecated address.
“This led to a loss of 15.99 million USDT which was absorbed by the company,” it said. The blog post does not call it a hack and does not say who was behind the irregular fund movement or how it happened.
CoinDesk has reached out to CoinDCX to ask whether it means the old, retired addresses were hacked again.
“We want to reiterate that all user funds remain safe in secure, segregated cold wallets, protected by multi-layer custody and offline security controls,” the exchange said. Cold wallets are kept offline by design.
“It took us some time to do the thorough review of the deprecated infrastructure and confirm the sequence of events. We could have been more proactive, but we shared this update as soon as we had the complete picture,” it added.

title: Bitcoin ETFs Snap Two-Week Losing Streak Despite Late-Week Slide - Decrypt
text:
Bitcoin ETFs ended a choppy week in the green, but only just.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $137.9 million on Friday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, their second straight day of outflows. The two-day slide totaled about $773.5 million, eating into a $1.07 billion inflow run from Monday through Wednesday.
Even so, the funds finished the week up roughly $301 million, snapping a two-week losing streak.
October, though typically a seasonally good month for Bitcoin holders, remains in the red. The funds briefly turned positive for the month midweek, but Thursday’s $635.6 million exit, the biggest of October, flipped them back. They’re now down about $314 million for the month. Cumulative net inflows stand at $57.6 billion, with $100.2 billion in total net assets.
Ethereum ETFs eked out a $4.4 million inflow on Friday but lost about $221 million on the week, leaving them down roughly $1.18 billion for October. Solana ETFs saw no net flows Friday after shedding $8.9 million Thursday, and they’re down about $68 million this month.
Spot crypto ETFs hold the underlying asset, such as Bitcoin or Ethereum, and trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares, giving investors exposure through a regular brokerage account. Bitcoin funds have drawn $57.6 billion in net inflows since debuting in January 2024, and Ethereum funds have taken in $12.7 billion since launching that July. Solana funds arrived late last year. Because issuers report flows daily and much of the money comes from institutions and financial advisers, the figures have become a closely watched gauge of investor sentiment.
Prices slid into the weekend. Bitcoin fell 1.1% over 24 hours to about $80,490 on Saturday and is down 1.2% on the week, according to CoinGecko.
Ethereum dropped 2.6% to roughly $2,344, Solana fell 2.8% to about $101, and total crypto market cap slipped 1.2% to $2.79 trillion. The weakness follows a midweek selloff in global markets, when oil climbed above $111 a barrel and AI stocks slid.
Traders on Myriad, a prediction market developed by Decrypt’s parent company Dastan, have grown more bearish on Bitcoin’s October finish. They now give Bitcoin a 43% chance of dropping to $77,500 before the month ends, up from 32% a day earlier, and an 18% chance of falling to $75,000.
The odds of Bitcoin topping $87,500 have fallen to 10% from 17%. Solana bulls barely edge out bears, with 51.6% odds of reaching $160 before $40, down from 54.9%. Ethereum’s odds of hitting $3,000 before $1,500 held at 61.3%.
The week opened on a brighter note, after J.P. Morgan Asset Management projected 10% annual returns for Bitcoin over the next decade, but Bitcoin has since settled into what analysts have described as a “wait-and-see” mode.

title: Crypto longs lose $404 million in four hours as bitcoin briefly slips below $80,000
text: Bitcoin briefly dropped below $80,000 on Saturday, and traders with leveraged bets on higher prices took most of the losses. Of the $436.44 million in positions liquidated in the four hours to 1 p.m. ET, $404.15 million were longs, per CoinGlass liquidation data. Most of the liquidations came in two bursts. Traders saw $208.21 million in longs liquidated in the 15 minutes from 10:15 a.m. ET, as bitcoin (BTC) fell from about $80,640 to $80,100, and another $131.17 million in the 15 minutes from 11:15 a.m., according to CoinGlass. Long liquidations between 8 a.m. and noon ET totaled $401.91 million. That was the most for any four-hour period since the night of Oct. 14, when $505.57 million in longs were wiped out. Bitcoin fell to about $79,280 around 11:20 a.m. ET before climbing back to $80,138 by 1 p.m., according to The Block's Bitcoin Price page. As BTC's price recovered, shorts made up $8.35 million of the $10.62 million liquidated in the hour to 1:09 p.m. ET. Bitcoin was down 1.9% over 24 hours, while ether (ETH) was down 3.8% at $2,314. Liquidations over the past 24 hours came to $815.26 million, up 218% from the previous day, with 201,012 traders hit, per the data. Open interest in crypto futures fell 2.2% to $140.10 billion over the same period. An exchange liquidates a leveraged position when the trader's margin can't cover the losses. Ether and Hyperliquid Ether positions accounted for $136.72 million of the four-hour total, against $158.45 million for bitcoin. Ether liquidations totaled $136.72 million, close to bitcoin’s $158.45 million, despite ether currently having only about 18% of bitcoin’s market capitalization. Longs made up 94.2% of bitcoin liquidations and 92.7% of ether's. The largest single liquidation order of the past 24 hours was an $11.85 million ETH-USDT long on Binance, closed at $2,307.65, per CoinGlass. Binance accounted for $226.07 million of the four-hour liquidations, 96% of them longs. On Hyperliquid, the onchain perpetual futures exchange, $70.47 million in positions were liquidated, and 99.8% of them were longs, per the data. Bitcoin ETFs record two days of net outflows U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs recorded $137.94 million in net outflows on Friday, according to The Block's analysis of SoSoValue data. BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $110.34 million of that, or 80%, and Fidelity's FBTC for $31.78 million, partly offset by $4.19 million in inflows to Morgan Stanley's MSBT. Friday's outflows came after an even worse day, with the funds logging $635.49 million in net outflows on Thursday. The funds had taken in $1.078 billion from Monday through Wednesday, which left them with $304.73 million in net inflows for the week. The funds held total net assets worth $104.43 billion as of Friday, roughly flat on the week. Spot ether ETFs had $4.35 million in net inflows on Friday, but those inflows were not enough to offset outflows from earlier in the week, with the funds logging $220.60 million in net outflows over the week. The ether funds have seen net outflows on 14 of 17 trading days in October, totaling $1.175 billion, SoSoValue data show. Bitcoin also slid on Thursday alongside a sell-off in tech stocks, The Block reported. Hayes 'dumped it all' BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes said early Saturday that he had closed out the directional book at Maelstrom, his family office. "I dumped it all," Hayes wrote on X at 2:18 a.m. ET, adding that he took profits on ETH, ENA, UNI "and other shitcoins." "I think we gotta go down to go up," Hayes wrote. "It looks a bit dicey out there in macro and geopolitical land." He said he would "sit on the sidelines and wait for the all clear signal." Hayes did not say which geopolitical risks he meant. The State Department is reducing staff at U.S. embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, the Associated Press reported late Friday. An internal memo cited increased Iranian efforts to target U.S. personnel, according to the AP.

title: Hong Kong Names Solana Company Strategic Enterprise
text:
The Nasdaq-listed firm said it plans to establish Solana validator operations in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong has named Nasdaq-listed Solana Company (HSDT) a strategic enterprise under a government program aimed at attracting businesses that support the city’s economic development.
Solana Company said Thursday that it was among the seventh batch of businesses selected by Hong Kong’s Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises (OASES) and the only blockchain infrastructure company onboarded by the office in 2026.
Hong Kong’s government confirmed the addition of 18 enterprises to the program last week, bringing its total to 142.
A Solana Company spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the designation gives it a single point of contact across government agencies and regulators, expedited pathways for recruiting overseas talent and introductions to local institutional partners.
Solana Company operates staking and validator infrastructure and advises financial institutions on blockchain adoption. It also holds Solana (SOL) as part of its digital asset treasury strategy.
The company said it plans to establish validator operations in Hong Kong under Pacific Backbone, an initiative to build a low-latency blockchain infrastructure network across the Asia-Pacific region.

title: Bitcoin wallet bug let rogue servers steal funds when users tried to speed up payments
text:
A bitcoin wallet security flaw allowed malicious servers to trick users into signing payments to attackers when they tried to speed up transactions, with developers confirming at least one case in which money was stolen.
Electrum, one of Bitcoin's oldest software wallets, disclosed the vulnerability on Saturday, saying some servers were already exploiting it. The developers received two reports in October, including one from a user who lost funds after approving what appeared to be a routine transaction-fee increase.
The attack exploited how Electrum handles bitcoin payments not yet confirmed by the network.
Unlike a full Bitcoin node, Electrum relies on outside servers to retrieve transaction histories and broadcast payments. Before the fix, the wallet trusted those servers to report pending transactions without verifying their signatures.
An attacker controlling one of those servers could intercept a payment before it reached the Bitcoin network and replace it in the wallet's history with a fake transaction. This replacement spent the user's coins to an attacker-controlled address, using invalid signatures that Electrum failed to detect.
But the wallet then showed the fake payment as pending, and the trap set in when users tried to speed things up.
Bitcoin allows unconfirmed transactions to be replaced with versions carrying higher fees, a feature called Replace-by-Fee. If a user selected that option, Electrum could take the fraudulent transaction and sign a valid replacement, sending the coins to the attacker.
In one reported case, the malicious transaction carried no fee at all, making it appear stuck. Attackers also generated receiving addresses whose last four characters matched the legitimate destination, making the substitution harder to spot during a quick check.
The first report, submitted Oct. 11, involved a two-of-three multisignature wallet using two Trezor hardware devices. The user had checked the legitimate payment on both devices but later noticed a different outgoing transaction in the wallet's history (that user did not report losing funds).
A second user reported on Oct. 18 that they had raised the fee on a substituted transaction and lost money. Developers have not disclosed the amount stolen or identified the malicious servers.
In response, Electrum released version 4.8.3 on Oct. 24, adding signature checks for unconfirmed transactions spending coins from the user's own wallet. However, earlier versions remain vulnerable to the reported attack when connected to malicious servers.
The developers recommend upgrading and checking receiving addresses and amounts before signing payments. Users connected only to servers they trust, including their own, were not exposed to this attack.
The fix came six days after the first reported theft.

title: Google Quietly Updates Privacy Policy to Let Gmail and Photos Data Feed Ads - Decrypt
text:
Google has carved out an exception to its long-standing promise not to use Gmail, Drive, and Google Photos content for advertising, quietly revising its privacy policy so that data from those apps can help personalize ads when users connect it to the company’s AI features.
The change, which took effect Oct. 16 and was first spotted by Android Authority, adds a conditional clause to a pledge Google has made for years.
The updated policy now reads that Google doesn’t show personalized ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”
The catch hinges on Personal Intelligence, Google’s push to make its AI tools more useful by letting features like AI Mode in Search and Gemini draw on a user’s own data.
Connecting Gmail, Drive or Photos to those tools delivers more tailored answers, such as surfacing a hotel reservation buried in an inbox. But under the revised wording, that same connected data can now also inform which ads a person sees.
Google stressed the limits. Content from the three services still isn’t used for ad targeting by default, advertisers don’t get access to the contents of anyone’s Gmail, Drive or Photos, and the company says it won’t share personally identifying details without permission.
In practice, that means Google isn’t scanning private emails and photos wholesale to sell ads, but users who opt into its AI conveniences may be trading some ad privacy for them.
Users can opt out by disconnecting the apps under Connected Content apps in their Google Account’s Data & privacy settings, or by turning off personalized recommendations, though Android Authority noted that previously collected data may linger in a user’s Search history even after disconnecting.
The quiet rollout echoes recent Google privacy posturing around its AI ambitions. As Decrypt reported in May, Google’s Chrome browser began silently installing a multi-gigabyte on-device AI model on users’ computers, and separately removed a privacy claim tied to its Gemini Nano model, both moves that drew scrutiny over how the company handles user data as it races to embed AI across its products.

title: Argentine judge clears Milei and 10 others in LIBRA case, finding no 'criminally relevant deception'
text: An Argentine federal judge on Friday dismissed the criminal case against President Javier Milei over his promotion of the LIBRA token, ruling that the events under investigation "do not fit any legal offense" for Milei and 10 others. Judge Marcelo Martínez de Giorgi's 60-page ruling clears Milei, his sister Karina Milei, who is the presidency's secretary general, and nine others. Among them are Hayden Davis, the American who described himself as LIBRA's "launch adviser," crypto lobbyist Mauricio Novelli, and Julian Peh of KIP Protocol. The ruling follows prosecutor Eduardo Taiano's request for the dismissal of the case. None of the 11 people investigated was called to give a formal statement as a suspect in the case. Milei posted about LIBRA on X on the evening of Feb. 14, 2025, before the token spiked in value, then deleted the post following the token's sudden crash. Milei later said he had acted in good faith. The token's market cap topped $4.5 billion before falling about 95% mere hours after the token's rise, and eight wallets tied to the team cashed out $107 million, according to onchain analysts. Judge finds no 'criminally relevant deception' The judge sided with the prosecutor, Taiano, finding that the evidence did not establish "criminally relevant deception" by Milei or his co-defendants. Milei's office "could have conferred particular repercussion and visibility" on the token, he wrote in Spanish. But the notoriety of whoever promotes an asset and the publicity around a launch "do not, in themselves, amount to a fraudulent scheme," the judge found. The judge also examined a note recovered from Novelli's phone that, according to El Destape's reporting in March, described three payments totaling $5 million. Forensic analysis confirmed that the note had existed in Apple Notes but could not establish that it had been sent to Davis or anyone else, the judge wrote. Investigators also found deleted chats with a contact saved as "Karina Milei RRPP" and records of calls between Milei and Novelli but could not determine their content. On Karina Milei, the judge found that the only paper trail linking her to Davis was the presidency's record of her authorizing his entry to the Casa Rosada, the Argentine president's seat of government, on July 16, 2024. That authorization, "considered in isolation, does not demonstrate the existence of an illicit agreement," the judge wrote. Separately, he cited an internal disciplinary investigation that found an employee of DATIP, the prosecutors' forensic unit, had improperly accessed reserved case files, some of which leaked to the press. Milei cheers while opposition alleges a cover-up Milei cheered the dismissal of the case with an X post on Friday evening. " Justice has once again put things in their place, exposing the TREMENDOUS political and media operation whose sole aim was to damage the presidential office for coup-mongering political ends," Milei wrote. Maximiliano Ferraro, the opposition deputy who chaired Congress' LIBRA investigative commission, responded to the ruling with a video posted to X. " We are facing a clear planned judicial operation of cover-up and impunity for Milei and all the organizers of the scam," Ferraro wrote in Spanish. "They never explained, nor were they ever required to explain, the dozens of meetings that $LIBRA's promoters held at the Casa Rosada and the Quinta de Olivos, the cryptocurrency transactions before and after meeting with the president of the nation, and the calls by Milei... on the day of the scam," Ferraro said in the video. The Ferraro-led commission's report, released in November 2025, found that Milei had provided "essential collaboration" to the project. Judge Martínez de Giorgi's ruling does not mention it. Plaintiffs seek path to appeal Taiano is not expected to appeal the ruling, per Perfil, and no private plaintiffs remain in the case. In July, at the request of Novelli's lawyers, Martínez de Giorgi removed five investors who had joined as plaintiffs from the case. Appeals judges Mariano Llorens and Pablo Bertuzzi upheld that on Sept. 4, writing that LIBRA buyers "voluntarily assumed the risks inherent in that type of purchase." The investors have since gone to the Federal Criminal Cassation Court, according to La Política Online, asking to be added back to the case. If that court reinstates them, they could appeal Friday's dismissal. On July 15, 12 days after the plaintiffs were removed, Milei and Justice Minister Juan Bautista Mahiques signed a decree naming Martínez de Giorgi's wife, Ana María Cristina Juan, to a federal court, Infobae reported. The Senate had approved Juan's nomination before the decree was signed. Opposition lawmakers, including Unión por la Patria deputy Sabrina Selva, questioned the appointment in their criticisms of Friday's ruling, per Ámbito. The Block has reached out to the Office of the President and to representatives for Davis for comment.

title: NY Seeks $1.37 Billion Judgment Against NovaTech Operators
text:
Two successive crypto frauds took investors for more than $1.1 billion. Now New York's attorney general is asking a court to make the operators pay it back — with interest.
New York Attorney General Letitia James is trying to secure a $1.37 billion judgment against the operators of NovaTech and its predecessor AWS Mining, two successive cryptocurrency investment schemes that allegedly defrauded hundreds of thousands of investors worldwide out of more than $1 billion.
Alleged founders Cynthia and Eddy Petion never appeared in court and, according to the AG’s office, fled the country.
“NovaTech and AWS Mining scammed thousands of vulnerable New Yorkers by telling them they were making a safe investment when in reality, they were victims of a pyramid scheme,” James said in a statement. “These scammers targeted immigrant and religious communities with the promise of a better life but instead robbed them of their life savings.”
The schemes, AWS Mining and later NovaTech, relied on promoters who recruited heavily in Haitian and other immigrant communities — through prayer groups, WhatsApp chats, and ads in Haitian Creole.
AWS Mining sold crypto mining contracts promising 15 to 20 percent monthly returns and 200 percent within 15 months. It collapsed in 2019. The Petions then launched NovaTech, marketed as a registered hedge fund broker, promising weekly trading returns of two to four percent — more than 140 percent a year.
Those returns were fabricated, according to prosecutors. Records from B2Broker, which supplied NovaTech’s white-label trading platform, show that of the more than $1 billion investors deposited between 2019 and 2023, only about $26 million was ever actually traded — and NovaTech’s traders lost $18.2 million of that. Returns to earlier investors came from newer deposits, not trading. When NovaTech collapsed in mid-2023, tens of thousands of investors could not withdraw their funds.
The AG is also seeking $134.5 million the Petions allegedly withdrew to their own wallets from the investor account Cynthia Petion solely controlled, plus $4.7 million tied to the earlier AWS Mining scheme. A default judgment entered in August 2025 already bars the couple and their companies from the securities, commodities, and cryptocurrency industries.
Separately, four of the scheme’s top promoters have agreed to pay nearly $6 million in disgorgement to victims and accepted the same industry bans.

title: Keystone Breach Exposes Hardware Wallet Buyers’ Addresses
text:
A security researcher warned that the leaked shipping details could expose crypto holders to targeted scams and physical attacks.
Crypto hardware wallet maker Keystone has disclosed a website security breach that exposed customer information to attackers, raising concerns about targeted scams and physical attacks.
Keystone said Saturday that it detected suspicious activity earlier in the week and confirmed Friday, after reviewing API activity with Shopify, that an unauthorized third party had accessed customer shipping information. This included names, contact details, shipping addresses and other order details, such as items bought.
“We’ve blocked access, fixed the vulnerability, opened an investigation, and are emailing affected customers,” said the company.
Keystone warned that the exposed information could be used for targeted phishing attacks. However, security researcher Taylor Monahan also raised concerns that leaking shipping addresses could expose customers to physical attacks and kidnappings.
Blockchain security firm CertiK recorded 52 verified wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up 33% from 39 during the same period last year. Such crimes, commonly called “wrench attacks,” involve using physical threats or violence to force cryptocurrency holders to surrender their assets.
“Again, we’re truly sorry to everyone affected,” Keystone said. The company did not disclose how many customers were impacted.
The breach has also raised questions about Keystone’s handling of older customer information.
In a 2023 blog post, Keystone said it had reduced its customer data retention period to 180 days following security incidents affecting other hardware wallet manufacturers.
However, some customers said they received breach notifications despite purchasing their devices more than two years ago, raising questions about what information Keystone retained and whether the notifications indicate that older order records were not deleted as promised.
Related: Italy investigates government email breach linked to Revolut data leak
An X user going by “OG DEGEN” said they received a call from a scammer claiming they were law enforcement investigating a fraud case. The user suspected the caller obtained their information through a Keystone order placed in 2024, based on the personal information the caller referred to.
“I think their plan was to convince me that my private keys had been exposed and then send me a phishing link to supposedly reset them,” they wrote on X.
Another X user, trintaetres, also said they received the email notification despite buying the device over two years ago.
Cointelegraph contacted Keystone to ask how customer information from purchases made more than 180 days earlier could have been exposed despite its previously announced retention policy, and how many customers were affected. The company did not respond by publication time.

title: Bitcoin slips under $80,000 as traders de-risk ahead of Fed meeting
text:
Bitcoin fell nearly 2% to about $79,800 as of Monday Asian morning hours as traders cut risk ahead of this week’s Federal Reserve meeting and another leg down in the AI trade weighed on tech stocks across the region.
Selling hit almost every major token. Ether dropped nearly 3% to just above $2,300, and XRP lost about 3% to $1.28. SOL slid 2% and is barely holding $100. DOGE, ZEC, HYPE and BNB each fell 1% to 2%, while TRX was the only major in the green, up less than 1%, according to CoinDesk data.
“This week, all eyes are on the Fed meeting and it already seems like investors are de-risking as Bitcoin falls below the $80k mark. While the Fed probably won’t change rates this week, we’re watching how strongly the chair hints at a December hike — that’s what matters for crypto,” Jeff Mei, chief operating officer at crypto exchange BTSE, said in an email to CoinDesk.
“Given record high oil prices, the escalating US-Iran conflict, and inflation, the Fed could very well adopt an aggressive tone, which means higher rates and less liquidity for crypto and stocks,” he added.
The Fed announces its decision on Wednesday, and traders will be listening to Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference for any hint that a hike is coming in December. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and tend to pull money out of riskier assets like crypto.
In Asia, the AI selloff kept going. South Korea’s Kospi, which traders watch for AI sentiment because of how much weight chipmakers like Samsung Electronics carry in it, fell 1% after Goldman Sachs strategists cut their 12-month target for the index by 25%. Chip stocks were the biggest losers on Japan’s Nikkei, and Chinese AI model developers slumped. Nasdaq 100 futures slipped 0.1% as investors braced for earnings from the biggest U.S. tech companies this week.
The MSCI Asia Pacific Index fell 0.1%, and it’s struggling to recover from four straight weeks of losses, its longest losing run since April.
Oil gave markets a bit of relief. Brent crude fell 2% from a six-month high to about $114 a barrel after President Donald Trump said it’s “getting to be decision time” on whether to reach a deal with Iran or resume attacks. Treasuries rose.
Bitcoin needs to get back above $82,500, the floor it lost last Thursday, before buyers can call this week’s dip a pause.

title: Sweden's Government Offices Block ChatGPT and Claude, Keep Microsoft Copilot - Decrypt
text:
Sweden's Government Offices—the administrative body supporting the prime minister and cabinet—will block ChatGPT and Claude on staff computers from Monday, directing civil servants to Microsoft's Copilot as the only approved AI tool, according to Sweden’s national, publicly funded radio broadcaster Sveriges Radio.
The reasoning comes from Mikael Wettercrantz, the Government Offices' director of digitalisation, who posted on the staff intranet that using AI services without a formal contract can have "consequences for our information security."
“We have seen several examples of problematic use of open AI services. The examples concern both the sensitivity of the information that has been entered and how the AI-generated responses have been handled,” he said.
Consumer AI tools without formal agreements send user queries to external company servers—and U.S. law allows authorities to compel those companies to hand over data on request.
A formal security agreement, at minimum, defines what the provider can and cannot do with government employees' inputs, which is why the distinction between a vetted enterprise contract and an open consumer tool matters here.
Copilot passes because the Government Offices reviewed it and raised its security settings after the review—something it did not do for ChatGPT or Claude. Some employees can still access both blocked tools through an AI platform the Government Offices built internally, though the press office hasn't said how many people that covers or what restrictions apply.
Sweden's Tax Agency and the National Board of Institutional Care have already imposed similar bans on consumer AI tools. The Enforcement Authority—the agency responsible for debt collection and enforcing court orders—is preparing a decision of its own. An internal audit at the Transport Administration separately found roughly 10 AI services being used there in a "widespread and risky way."
The European Parliament went further in February, disabling AI features across all its work devices—ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot included—after concluding it could not guarantee the security of data those tools processed.
European government concerns about AI data security have been building since Italy's ChatGPT ban in 2023. Sweden is now drawing a narrower line than Brussels, sanctioning one U.S. tech company's product while shutting out two others.
Microsoft incorporated Claude models into Copilot in early 2026. In the EU—where Sweden sits—Anthropic's models default to off and require administrators to deliberately enable them.
Sweden's Government Offices has not confirmed whether its Copilot instance has Claude switched on, which means the distinction between the "banned" AI and the "approved" one is not as clean as the announcement implies.

title: Standard Chartered-Backed Anchorpoint Eyes Retail Stablecoin
text:
The Standard Chartered and Animoca Brands joint venture previously targeted retail access as early as the end of 2026, but its CEO declined to reaffirm that timeline.
Standard Chartered-backed stablecoin venture Anchorpoint says it will take a cautious approach to opening its Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin to retail users, declining to confirm a launch date after rival HSBC rolled out RedCoin, according to the South China Morning Post.
The venture released its institutional stablecoin product in August and previously indicated a retail offering could arrive as early as the end of 2026.
Anchorpoint CEO Dominic Maffei declined to confirm that timeline at a Friday press conference, saying the company would take a prudent approach.
“We believe it’s important to build the market out in a long-term, sustainable manner,” Maffei said, adding that rushing a launch “does not make sense.”
The update comes after HSBC launched its Hong Kong dollar-backed RedCoin on Friday for the 3.3 million users of its PayMe app.
Anchorpoint grew out of a partnership between Standard Chartered, Animoca Brands and telecommunications provider HKT, which was announced in February 2025, following their joint participation in Hong Kong’s stablecoin issuer sandbox in July 2024.
Animoca’s role is to bring its blockchain expertise and industry network to the venture and help develop uses for the stablecoin across the Web3 ecosystem.

title: Netanyahu seeking blockchain plan to prepare for possible sanctions
text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he has asked for a plan involving blockchain to help the country prepare for possible economic sanctions, including banking restrictions. "We need to understand that there could be sanctions, including banking sanctions. You need to prepare an economy that can bypass them," Netanyahu said in an interview broadcast Friday on Israel's Channel 10, according to a translation of the Hebrew transcript. "You know what that means, and you know about the currencies that bypass this. I'm working on that too. There are other things as well." The interviewer, Roy Katz, then asked whether Netanyahu saw blockchain as an alternative for dealing with economic sanctions on Israel. "One of them, certainly. I have already asked for a plan to be prepared for that," Netanyahu replied. Netanyahu did not say who would prepare the plan, which blockchain or currencies it might involve, or when it could be implemented. Netanyahu said Israel also needs to prepare for an eventual end to U.S. military assistance. Referring to the tens of billions of dollars in aid he said he had secured, he warned that such support would not continue indefinitely. "It's only a matter of time," he said. Netanyahu said Israel must build not only its military strength but also its ability to independently manufacture ammunition and weapons. He said he had allocated an additional 400 billion shekels, or around $129 billion, to the defense budget over the coming years. He also said Israel should prepare for a less favorable U.S. political environment after President Donald Trump leaves office. "I can tell you with certainty: there has never been a president this friendly, and it's doubtful there will ever be another like him," Netanyahu said.

title: Elon Musk issues a warning for AI neoclouds as SpaceX borrows $40 billion
text:
Nasdaq-listed SpaceX SPCX has raised $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, the powerful processors used to run artificial-intelligence systems.
Elon Musk announced the deal on X, pairing it with a warning for neoclouds — companies whose revenue depends almost entirely on data centers — that could add to AI jitters on Wall Street and risk aversion in broader financial markets, including cryptocurrencies.
The $40 billion deal is mainly callable debt, meaning SpaceX can repay it early. The money could be used to pay for GPU deliveries expected in the first half of 2027, though Musk did not explicitly say so. Reuters previously reported that SpaceX was negotiating with banks and asset managers to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia AI chips.
Musk said the reason SpaceX could borrow the money is because it has a strong credit rating and steady revenue from Starlink internet service and rocket launches. Those businesses do not depend on AI data centers, making it easier for SpaceX to secure chip financing than for companies that rely entirely on data centers for revenue. Debt funding for such firms is drying up, Musk noted.
“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” he said on X.
Musk predicted that more than 200 “neoclouds” — newer companies that rent out AI computing power — will consolidate, with only a few surviving.
The episode shows how costly the AI computing race has become. Building large clusters of AI chips can require tens of billions of dollars. Companies with diverse revenue and strong credit can still borrow; firms whose entire business depends on AI infrastructure face a tougher time as lenders become more selective.
Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya had earlier said many neoclouds appear poorly funded and badly run. He argued that Amazon, Microsoft and Google are moving slowly on deals and prefer to keep computing power for their own use. He said delays in building data centers could leave many chips and half-finished projects sitting idle or failing to earn enough to cover financing costs in 2027.
Lately, financial markets have become increasingly worried about the payoff from massive AI spending. That has pressured AI-linked stocks and the broader market. Nasdaq futures traded near 29,080 as of this writing, down sharply from above 30,000 early this month.

title: Game Publishers Have Pushed to Cut Discs Since 2007, Infinity Ward Veteran Says - Decrypt
text:
Video game publishers have attempted to stop physical disc production and go fully digital for almost two decades, a former Infinity Ward employee told Decrypt. Ultimately, he said, the movement was an attempt by publishers to maximize profits and fight back against the resale market.
Robert Bowling, former Infinity Ward creative strategist for the Call of Duty franchise from 2006 to 2012, told Decrypt that he first heard conversations about cutting discs as far back as 2007—during the production of Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare.
"At one point, it was floated by an executive at Activision [the Call of Duty publisher] that if we went entirely digital and stopped printing on discs, they could avoid the resell conversation entirely, and they'd control the market for their games," Bowling told Decrypt. "It would also evade the disc fee charged by Xbox and PlayStation to have your game on an Xbox disc or PlayStation disc."
Bowling added that behind the scenes, publishers were attempting to convince GameStop to share its revenue from second-hand games. That battle was won by GameStop, so publishers looked to cut discs to kill the resale market entirely.
"It was at that point that I raised the concern that we'd be trading the freedom and joy of collecting games purely for a profit increase," he said. "That felt counter to our culture as gamers and game developers."
It comes amid controversy over Sony's decision to discontinue discs as of 2028. The move has attracted pushback from consumers, with more than 387,000 people signing a "Don't Kill the Disc" petition. Meanwhile, PlayStation founder Ken Kutaragi came to Sony's defence, claiming that it's a "mentality issue" if gamers are upset by the decision to cut discs.
After six years at Infinity Ward, Bowling went on to work on several other major titles like Battlefield V, Apex Legends, and Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order as a creative consultant at Electronic Arts. In 2021, Bowling co-founded Midnight Society to build crypto extraction shooter Deadrop, but left in 2025 as funding ran dry. Now, he is studio head of //18.bravo, which is currently developing a first-person shooter.
Bowling told Decrypt that throughout his two decades in the video game industry, publishers have been the "only ones" pushing to cut physical discs. This is because, he said, publishers are motivated by increasing their profit margins, by reducing production costs, and squashing the second-hand game market.
"It speaks to the divide that has formed in our industry between those who see games as just a software product and those who see them as something more like art, entertainment, as collectibles, and a lifestyle," Bowling said.
The only reason Sony didn’t make the move back in 2007 is that consumer habits have since flipped, he said, as more gamers buy digital over physical.
Sony argues that purchasing a digital game from the PlayStation Store does not constitute ownership of that game, according to court filings. Rather, Sony says, Store purchases equate to a license that can be revoked at any time.
"Whether our players actually own the games they purchase from us matters," Bowling said. "As developers, we are making games to be purchased and enjoyed. We want you to own, share, and cherish those games. It's publishers, like Sony, that are pushing the pure business side of the industry, and ignoring how impactful the end result is to our lives."
Activision did not immediately respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

title: Sen. Blumenthal seeks answers from Tether over payments to firm founded by ex-White House crypto adviser
text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal said he wants answers from Tether following reports that the stablecoin issuer paid millions of dollars to a consulting firm started by former White House crypto adviser Bo Hines and his father amid negotiations to pass stablecoin legislation into law. The Connecticut Democrat said that relationship raised legal and ethical concerns, in a letter sent to Tether and Hines. "Tether’s alleged multimillion-dollar payment to a firm controlled by the White House official primarily responsible for cryptocurrency policy implicates federal ethics, anticorruption, and lobbying laws," Blumenthal said on Thursday. Last week, The Wall Street Journal reported that Tether had started a business relationship with Nxum — a consulting firm started by Bo Hines and his father — weeks after Hines took the helm as the White House's top crypto advisor. During Hines' time at the White House, he played a pivotal role in passing the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins, or GENIUS Act, which created the first federal regulatory framework for stablecoins. Tether, which issues the world's largest stablecoin, became an advocate for the GENIUS Act and, through it, launched the U.S.-based version of its flagship stablecoin, called USAT. A Tether spokesperson told The Block that the company is reviewing the letter. "Tether is aware of the allegations reported in The Wall Street Journal that form the basis of Senator Blumenthal’s letter," the spokesperson said. "External counsel previously conducted an in-depth internal investigation into the matter, which found no evidence of wrongdoing." Lawmakers, including Blumenthal, have repeatedly scrutinized Tether over the past year. Last month, Blumenthal released findings of an investigation that found that Tether had become central in "Iran's shadow banking system" and the financing activities of terrorist groups. Tether has pushed back and said it helps authorities find bad actors. In Blumenthal's latest letter, he asked Tether to provide records involving the stablecoin issuer's business dealings with Nxum as well as with Hines. Blumenthal also sent a letter on Thursday to Nxum. Harry Jung, the now-former deputy director of the President's Council of Advisors for Digital Assets who worked with Hines, is now at Nxum, according to his X account. Leadership at the council is also absent now following the departure of Patrick Witt last week after his detail expired. Witt did not say where he would be going next, but said in a post on X that he looked forward to advancing his mission in the private sector.

title: AI Agents Rescue ETH’s Glamsterdam Fork, ‘Steal My Bitcoin’ Site: Hodler’s Digest
text:
Similar to the Hugging Face hack, Ethereum researchers have set up an AI Agent message board to help rescue the Glamsterdam fork. ‘Steal My Bitcoin’ site successfully hacked.
The second and final testnet for Ethereum’s Glamsterdam hard fork was cancelled this week, after ChainSecurity found vulnerabilities in two gas scaling Ethereum Improvement Proposals that could have spelled big trouble for at least 13 DeFi contracts.
The bugs were connected to EIP-8037/8038 and resulted in contracts, that rely on the way gas currently behaves, breaking when a call runs out of gas. It’s all fairly technical and complicated, but the upshot is that an attacker may have been able to exploit the resulting vulnerabilities.
The hard fork testnet dress rehearsal on Hoodi is not expected to be rescheduled until all the second order effects of the fork have been gamed out properly. In an article on X today, Derek Chiang from Ethlabs noted the issues were found very late in the process, which is less than ideal, “causing everyone to scramble to deal with the fallout.”
Chiang says two researchers from Ethlabs and the Ethereum Foundation had independently spun up a bunch of AI Agents to scan contracts for vulnerabilities. When they realized they were both employing the same strategy they “set up a message board for their agents in the form of a github repo” to coordinate the work.
He noted the similarities to the OpenAI <> Hugging Face hack where rogue agents had set up a message board to coordinate the attacks. “Well, turns out the same pattern is useful for the good agents too,” he said. The exercise has been so successful at finding potential problems that a second board has been set up to examine the effects of EIP-8198, aka “Quick Slots”, which has been proposed for the subsequent Hegota hard fork.
Updated October 26 12.10am UTC with the result of the challenge.
A website that challenged users to “Steal My Bitcoin” by exploiting unpatched PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, was successfully hacked within the space of a day. The site owner hid the key to a Bitcoin wallet worth around $2000 which was accessible to the PHP user account through a binary called print-flag.
The site generated a huge amount of interest and went offline periodically offline due to heavy traffic and probing attempts. It was solved by KillerBoi who successfully extracted the private key — however in a plot twist, the key could not access the wallet address shown on the site. Challenge organizer James Pavur acknowledged this was a mistake and said the funds would be transferred.
WordFence founder Mark Maunder said the despite the key being extracted within a day: “This is the absolute best explanation you’ll see on how hard #php2shell is to exploit. The author had to trigger a precise memory corruption condition, leak internal memory addresses, bypass aslr, reverse engineer php’s internal memory structures, forge structures to hijack execution, and account for php build differences, worker behavior and timing.”
PHP is a programming language widely used to power websites and web applications, including content management systems. Government agencies and other organizations in the Netherlands, Australia, Japan, Finland and elsewhere took critical websites offline Wednesday as a precaution while emergency patches were developed for two related critical vulnerabilities. The flaws could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers without logging in.

However, Poinsot said LLMs have made some flaws so easy to rediscover that delaying fixes offers little protection.

Blockstream Launches Institutional Consulting Services, Opens Lugano Office
text:
Blockstream will offer its engineering expertise to banks and asset managers from a new Swiss base.
Blockstream has launched a consulting business for financial institutions and opened an office in Lugano, Switzerland, the company shared today. The expansion gives banks, asset managers and other institutions direct access to the firm’s engineering teams and Bitcoin infrastructure, Blockstream said.
Blockstream Consulting Services will support institutions through the evaluation, design and implementation of Bitcoin-based financial infrastructure. The company said the business will develop solutions for tokenized asset issuance, confidential settlement and related infrastructure, with services spanning technical strategy, system architecture, integration and implementation.
From Lugano, Blockstream plans to serve clients across Switzerland, including Zurich, Geneva and Zug. The company said the office will serve as a hub for its European operations, supporting client relationships, strategic partnerships and collaboration with the region’s financial and technology communities.
“Switzerland is an important market for Blockstream given its longstanding banking tradition and supportive regulatory framework for digital assets,” said Peter Bain, chief marketing officer of the company. “We look to provide regional expertise in markets where we see demand for Bitcoin infrastructure. Our consulting business, combined with our new office in Lugano, will bring tailored Bitcoin solutions to financial institutions across Europe.”
Founded in 2014, Blockstream develops technology and services across Bitcoin custody, settlement, payments, asset issuance and self-custody. Its products include the Liquid Network sidechain, Elements, Simplicity, Core Lightning, the Jade hardware wallet and the Blockstream App. This year, the company launched Simplicity smart contracts on Liquid and added Lightning support to Jade.
The company said the consulting business draws on that experience, with capabilities in cryptography, protocol engineering, security and financial technology. Multidisciplinary teams will give institutions access to the firm’s technical staff from initial evaluation through deployment.
“The next phase of Bitcoin adoption is its integration into existing financial systems,” said Adam Back, Blockstream’s co-founder and CEO. “Our extensive experience in Bitcoin cryptography, protocol development and engineering gives Blockstream the technical expertise to address the complexities of integrating Bitcoin into traditional financial infrastructure.”
The company framed the move as part of a long-term commitment to Switzerland and a broader strategy of building a presence in key markets to support institutional Bitcoin adoption.
The country has become a center for digital asset firms, with Zug’s “Crypto Valley” and a regulatory framework that permits banks to hold and trade bitcoin on behalf of clients.
There was no pricing disclosed, headcount for the Lugano office or named clients for the consulting business. The company said the Lugano office is open and that consulting engagements are available to institutions across Europe.

title: Hong Kong’s Biggest Bank Puts a Stablecoin in 3 Million Wallets - Decrypt
text:
Banking giant HSBC switched on RedCoin on Friday, a Hong Kong dollar stablecoin that more than 3.3 million PayMe users will be able to activate in the coming days to pay friends or shop at more than 100,000 merchants, according to the bank's announcement.
“We are excited by the market's interest in HSBC RedCoin. This is only the beginning,” John O'Neill, HSBC's managing director of digital assets and currencies, said. “We will soon add more products, including expanding into wholesale corporate and institutional use cases.”
A stablecoin is a crypto token designed to always be worth one unit of a regular currency, so one RedCoin (ticker RCHKD) should equal one Hong Kong dollar. In practice, someone in Hong Kong can now pay for lunch with blockchain-based money issued by the same bank that may already hold their salary, without ever opening a crypto exchange.
Until now, stablecoins have mostly been a crypto-company business. Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC dominate a market worth more than $300 billion, and most of that money lives on trading platforms, not at the corner noodle shop.
HSBC got its issuer license from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, in April, under a regime that took effect in August 2025. It beat a crowded field of at least 36 companies competing by September of that year.
HSBC's reserve tracker showed roughly $10.2 million in RedCoin circulating shortly after launch—pocket change next to USDT—backed by $10.4 million held entirely in cash.
RedCoin also runs on HSBC's own private ledger rather than a public blockchain like Ethereum, and balances can't even move between PayMe and HSBC's banking app. It isn't a bank deposit either, so Hong Kong's Deposit Protection Scheme, the statutory insurance on savings accounts, doesn't cover it.
Later this year, HSBC plans to bring the token to its HK Mobile Banking app, where customers will be able to buy into a tokenized share class of its long-running Hong Kong dollar money market fund (a low-risk fund that parks cash in short-term debt). Tokenized simply means ownership is recorded as a digital token on a ledger instead of in a traditional registry.
Other banks want the same slice of everyday payments. In September, 21 lenders including Goldman Sachs and Bank of America announced plans for a joint dollar stablecoin, targeting a launch in the first half of 2027.
HSBC says the first independent attestation of RedCoin's reserves, an outside auditor's report confirming the cash is really there, is expected after the fourth quarter of 2026.

title: Initia halts network after security incident as attacker reportedly mints tokens

Co-founder Ezaan Mangalji, who goes by Zon, said preliminary findings pointed to a previously unknown " Day 0" bug in the network’s MoveVM implementation on Cosmos SDK that allowed unauthorized token minting but "does not apply to native INIT tokens." "The attacker was able to mint and bridge out ~$2.7m worth of AUSD, ETH, and USDC before the chain was paused," he said. Blockchain researcher Spreek initially estimated that the attacker had cashed out roughly $2.6 million and had more funds in transit. Initia exploiter's outbound ETH transaction. Source: Etherscan. Initia said it was investigating the reach of the incident alongside security teams, validators, and exchanges. It has not confirmed the amount lost. Initia's native INIT token fell 14% immediately after the exploit was reported, before reversing the losses. The token is now up 14% on the day. This is a developing story. title: ECB’s Cipollone Says Digital Euro a Matter of Sovereignty
text:
Piero Cipollone said the bloc is on track to test real transactions in 2027 and roll out a digital euro as early as 2029, pending legislation this year.
European Central Bank Executive Board member Piero Cipollone said the digital euro that is set for a pilot next year has the potential to give the bloc “sovereignty” over a payments infrastructure that currently requires dependency on external, non-European third parties.
Cipollone said in an interview with Italy’s Milano Finance published by the central bank on Saturday that because the bloc is critically dependent on third parties, it’s not easy to ensure this smooth functioning. He did not cite specific third parties.
“In recent years Europe has learned that, for some essential services, we cannot rely only on third parties. We saw this with energy and we’re seeing it today with defense. And the same is true for payments,” he said.
The pilot will use real transactions by ECB and national central bank staff. With 36 market operators, including seven from Italy, collaborating on preparations, the ECB is inviting e-commerce and mobile-commerce operators to participate.
“The smooth functioning of payment systems is one of our responsibilities. If we are critically dependent on third parties, it’s not easy to ensure this smooth functioning,” Cipollone said.
To be sure, sovereignty doesn’t mean shutting third parties out, Cipollone said. “It means having the power to choose and knowing that, for an essential service like payments, Europe can also rely on its own strength.”
In an April public lecture held in Latvia, Cipollone said that Europe’s reliance on non-European payment providers creates a strategic vulnerability. He said two-thirds of euro-area card transactions are governed by non-European companies, and that the digital euro could reduce that dependence and provide European-controlled payment infrastructure.
The ECB Governing Council can only decide on issuing a digital euro only after legislative negotiations in Brussels conclude.
“We hope that the regulation will be adopted by the end of the year, enabling the ECB’s Governing Council to issue a formal decision on issuance,” Cipollone told Milano Finance .
