title: Interpol Recovers $105M in African Cybercrime Sweep That Shut Illegal Crypto Mines - Decrypt
text:
Law enforcement agencies from 21 countries arrested 1,462 suspects, disrupted 10,909 malicious networks and recovered more than $105 million in an Interpol-coordinated crackdown on cybercrime in Africa, the international police organization said on Thursday.
Operation Serengeti III ran from June 29 to August 31, 2026, targeting ransomware, online scams, business email compromise, digital extortion and other cyber-enabled fraud. Authorities identified 65,929 victims, and financial investigations linked the networks to losses of more than $385 million, according to Interpol.
🚨 Operation Serengeti III dismantles thousands of malicious cyber networks
One of Africa’s largest cybercrime enforcement operations has seen agencies from 21 countries:🔵 Arrest 1,462 suspects🔵 Disrupt 10,909 malicious networks🔵 Recover USD 105 million in illicit funds… pic.twitter.com/qtkofnnPEA
— INTERPOL (@INTERPOL_HQ) October 22, 2026
In Angola, investigators dismantled two illegal crypto mining centers, arresting nine people and seizing more than 2,000 mining devices along with six illegal power transformation stations. The seized electrical equipment alone was worth more than $1 million, Interpol said.
In Nigeria, a suspect was arrested over an international investment fraud scheme promoted through messaging apps. Investigators traced more than $2.4 million in suspected criminal proceeds, much of which was laundered through crypto transactions.
Ugandan authorities dismantled two transnational fraud rings and arrested 365 foreign nationals linked to online investment and pension scams aimed at victims in Asia. The rings ran a rotating call-center operation using scripts, fake trading platforms and fraudulent websites to persuade pensioners to invest in opportunities that did not exist.
Other arrests included a Nigerian suspect accused of running a phishing and business email compromise operation that collected around 2.1 million email addresses, and 30 suspects linked to a cybercrime operation in the Republic of Congo.
"Cybercrime networks operate without regard for borders, exploiting technology to target victims on an unprecedented scale," said Neal Jetton, Interpol's director of cybercrime.
Private-sector partners including Group-IB, Kaspersky, blockchain analytics firm Uppsala Security and Meta supported the operation. Several investigations remain active as authorities try to identify more suspects and trace illicit proceeds, Interpol said.
The operation follows Operation Catalyst, a joint Interpol and Afripol crackdown on terrorist financing and cybercrime in which authorities arrested 83 people across six African countries in 2025. That operation flagged $260 million in illicit crypto and fiat, of which $600,000 had been seized, and identified several high-value crypto wallets that Interpol said were "potentially linked" to terrorist financing.
An Interpol expert told Decrypt at the time that criminals were "increasingly" using crypto in Africa, but that it was not yet the main way most cybercrime proceeds were paid or settled.

title: Bank Of Korea Moves To Regulate Stablecoins Under Forex Law
text:
The Bank of Korea told lawmakers it will draft a forex law amendment this year to regulate stablecoins as a means of payment, a plan that points to tighter cross-border controls rather than legal-tender status.
The Bank of Korea plans to draft an amendment to the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act with the government before year-end that would regulate stablecoins as a means of payment, according to a written submission to the National Assembly’s annual audit reported by Korean outlet Digital Asset.
The central bank’s October 22 report, a follow-up to last year’s audit, says it is consulting with the government on measures to regulate cross-border transactions in virtual assets.
While building a monitoring system based on foreign exchange network reporting, the bank said, it plans to prepare the amendment with the government this year to regulate stablecoins as a means of payment, among other aims.
That is a plan to write a bill, not a bill in itself. There is no draft text, no named token and no passage date. And “means of payment” is a defined term in Korean forex law: an instrument whose cross-border movement must be reported.
On that reading, the amendment would put dollar stablecoins under the same controls as a wire to New York, not make them legal tender at a Seoul convenience store.
The BOK pointed to settlement outside the banking system, mixers and regulatory gaps around personal wallets as factors that ease illegal transactions. Bitcoin holders who self-custody in Korea should take note: the country’s capital controls are the reason the kimchi premium exists, and a tighter forex net around crypto would entrench those controls rather than ease them.
The forex work runs in parallel with the Digital Asset Basic Act, the licensing and stablecoin-issuance framework flagged alongside spot bitcoin ETF approval in the government’s 2026 growth strategy.
Financial Services Commission chairman Lee Eog-weon told lawmakers Thursday that consultations are in their final stage and the bill will follow as soon as possible, Bloomingbit reported.
The BOK said it will work with ministries to limit transactions that exploit the gap until that law exists.
The gap has a date attached. Korea’s crypto income tax is due to take effect January 1, 2027, according to The Block, after three postponements, and lawmakers have questioned taxing a market before the law defining it is passed.
Lee said Thursday the tax should “take various circumstances into full consideration,” per Yonhap. Democratic Party leader Kim Min-seok called Thursday for a “thorough final review,” a shift from a party that had insisted on 2027.
Two petitions, one to repeal the tax and one to defer it two years, each cleared the 50,000 signatures that force a legislative review.
The National Tax Service has not moved: it plans to finalize its draft tax notice by October 30, Digital Asset reported.

title: Blockchain Association pushes for crypto tax clarity as broader bill stalls
text: As progress stalls on a broader crypto regulation bill, the Blockchain Association is urging Congress to pass legislation to resolve uncertainty around taxes for digital assets. On Thursday, the crypto industry group, which represents over 100 firms, said current tax policy needs to be updated and is unworkable. The letter was sent to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. "Americans who use digital assets aren't asking for special treatment. They want to follow the law and pay the taxes they owe, but today's rules are often unclear and unworkable," said Lindsay Fraser, chief policy officer of the Blockchain Association. On the House side, lawmakers have been working on legislation — specifically the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act, which passed out of the House Ways and Means Committee last month. Overall, the bill sets out to establish clear federal tax rules for digital assets, including setting a threshold for taxes so people would not have to pay taxes on network fees if the fee is $10 or less. That bill isn't expected to be taken back up until after November elections. The Blockchain Association pointed to progress made on digital asset legislation, but also said tax regulations are essential. Over the past two years, Congress has been working to pass broader crypto legislation called the Clarity Act, but it has since stalled in the Senate after it failed in its first procedural vote last month. "Congress has made progress toward clear rules for digital assets," the group said. "That work cannot fully succeed without a tax framework that is clear, administrable, technology-neutral, and aligned with economic reality." Future crypto tax legislation should include a de minimis exemption, should protect taxpayer privacy and should extend wash sale rules to crypto, among other asks, the group said. "These principles provide a path toward stronger tax compliance, greater certainty for taxpayers and businesses, and a regulatory environment that keeps the next generation of financial innovation – and the jobs it creates – in the United States," Fraser said in the letter.

Ethereum Delays Glamsterdam Testnet Fork Over Gas Security Flaws - Decrypt
text:
Ethereum developers have postponed the planned activation of the network's Glamsterdam upgrade on its Hoodi test network after security firm ChainSecurity found problems with how the upgrade changes gas, the auditor said on Thursday.
"It has just been decided to delay the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet because of security impacts we identified," ChainSecurity wrote, adding that it had "already found 13 real-world examples" and was in responsible disclosure with the affected projects.
⚠️ It has just been decided to delay the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet because of security impacts we identified in this blog post: https://t.co/UCpy6Jp5Pa
We already found 13 real-world examples and are in responsible disclosure with the affected projects.Please…
— ChainSecurity (@chain_security) October 22, 2026
The upgrade had been due to go live on Hoodi on Monday. Node operators should revert to an older software release without the upgrade scheduled, or wait for their execution client team to release a new version that cancels it, Ethereum researcher Christine Kim said. Preston Van Loon, a developer on the Prysm consensus client, said a Prysm release removing the upgrade from Hoodi's schedule would follow the same day.
Gas is the fee paid for computing work on Ethereum. Glamsterdam changes how the network charges for creating and accessing stored data through two proposals, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, and introduces a separate pool of gas for creating new state.
According to ChainSecurity's analysis, those changes break assumptions that many contracts rely on when an external call fails. Some contracts use gas checks, or rely on the call running out of gas, to stop an attacker from deliberately supplying too little gas so that a valid operation fails and is recorded as a permanent failure, a tactic known as insufficient gas griefing.
Under Glamsterdam, gas can be refilled or returned to a contract after a failed call, and repricing can change how much gas a call needs, the firm found. "Even with unchanged contract code, a failure path that previously reverted can now complete," it wrote. ChainSecurity urged projects to check their contracts, saying the Ethereum Foundation is working out how many are affected.
Glamsterdam has already gone live on Sepolia, another Ethereum test network, which activated the upgrade on October 6 and began producing blocks with a gas limit of nearly 200 million, more than three times mainnet's 60 million. The upgrade also adds block-level access lists, which let computers check transactions in parallel, and moves the auction that decides who assembles each block into Ethereum's own rules.
Developers had aimed to ship Glamsterdam on mainnet by the end of 2026, ahead of Hegotá, the next upgrade, which is expected in 2027 and could add native privacy features. No new date has been set for the Hoodi fork.

title: Coinbase Ireland fined $3.6 million over customer fund segregation, oversight failures
text: The Central Bank of Ireland has fined Coinbase Ireland €3.25 million for breaches of customer fund safeguarding and outsourcing rules under the Electronic Money Regulations, the regulator said in a statement on Thursday. According to the statement, the exchange admitted the violations on Oct. 21 and accepted a reprimand alongside the fine, which was reduced from €4.65 million under a 30% settlement discount. The sanctions require High Court confirmation before taking effect. Coinbase said it had fully resolved the issues and that no customers lost money or were unable to access their funds. The company said it self-reported several of the problems to the central bank in January 2024 and has since strengthened its safeguarding controls. Coinbase incorporated its Irish subsidiary in Dublin in July 2018. The company received an e-money license from the central bank nearly a year later in 2019 and secured virtual asset service provider registration from the regulator in 2022. Customer funds The settlement notice published by the central bank said Coinbase's handling of customer funds, including daily safeguarding shortfalls, reached €5.2 million ($5.8 million) in 2024. The central bank said the exchange allowed customer funds to be mixed with money held by other Coinbase entities. For about 19 months, from March 2023 to October 2024, approximately 30 institutional clients deposited dollars into bank accounts held by Coinbase Inc., rather than accounts in the Irish entity's name. Funds belonging to some customers who migrated from Coinbase UK were also deposited into the UK entity's safeguarding account until Aug. 19, 2025. "CBIE could not demonstrate adequate internal control mechanisms to validate that Users' Funds were properly segregated and safeguarded because it was unable to accurately calculate how much it was obligated to safeguard on a daily basis," the notice read. The regulator said the failures could also have complicated the return of customer funds if Coinbase Ireland had become insolvent. "Had CBIE become insolvent when the above referenced breaches of their safeguarding obligations were in being, then Users may not have been able to promptly and fully regain their funds," the notice read. This represents a fundamental failure to meet the Central Bank's expectations regarding wind-down strategy. Overeliance on outsourcing Coinbase Ireland also relied heavily on its U.S. parent group's infrastructure without sufficient local expertise to oversee safeguarding, according to the notice. The central bank had raised governance concerns in letters issued in July 2022 and March 2023, but said the issues were not adequately resolved. "CBIE also committed serious outsourcing breaches, demonstrating a lack of appropriate skills and experience to oversee the activities of safeguarding undertaken by the OSP, which ultimately had a material impact on its ability to safeguard, further compounding the issues arising," the regulator wrote. The exchange appointed a safeguarding officer in December 2024. The regulator's notice said the company remediated the identified shortfall in June 2024 and implemented a fix for the underlying data issue in October 2024. The latest penalty follows a separate €21.5 million fine against Coinbase Europe in November 2025 after more than 30 million transactions went unmonitored, resulting in 2,708 late suspicious transaction reports.

title: Can Bitcoin Self-Custody Get Easier Without Becoming Less Safe?
text:
Recent hardware wallet security incidents have renewed debate over whether self-custody is suitable for beginners, as multisig and seedless designs carry their own risks.
Crypto executives are divided over whether self-custody was ever designed for beginners, while approaches such as multisignature wallets and seedless backups come with their own security and usability trade-offs.
“We don’t expect every driver to be a mechanic, and we shouldn’t expect everyone who wants to own their assets to become a security expert,” Safe Labs CEO Rahul Rumalla told Cointelegraph.
Making self-custody easier to use could be critical to Bitcoin’s broader adoption, as the ability to “be your own bank” remains one of its defining features.
Recent incidents involving Ledger and Coldcard have exposed weaknesses in hardware wallets, widely recommended as one of the safest ways to hold crypto because they keep private keys offline.
Implants in some Ledger devices stole recovery phrases, while a Coldcard firmware bug allowed attackers to recreate private keys and steal funds.
Related: Ledger’s early implant warnings deserved more action, Karpelès says
Michael Tanguma, CEO of Bitcoin custody provider Onramp, compared Bitcoin custody to personal computers in the 1970s, when users needed technical skills to assemble and operate them.
“Self-custody was never designed with newcomers in mind,” he told Cointelegraph.
He said simpler designs helped computers reach a wider audience and that Bitcoin custody now faces a similar challenge.
Trezor Model One, the world’s first hardware wallet, was released in 2014. Source: Trezor
Rumalla disagreed, saying self-custody was “always meant for everyone” and that “being able to own and control your assets is the whole point of crypto.”
He added that self-custody “does not mean doing everything yourself.”
Multisignature, or multisig, wallets require multiple keys to authorize transactions, but managing them can be difficult for beginners.
“Traditional multisig implementations can introduce additional complexity involving signer coordination, key backups, recovery procedures, and transaction approvals,” Justin Hutzler, chief technology officer of Synergy Network, said.
Single signature versus multisig. Source: BitGo
Multiple approvals also cannot prevent every attack.
Safe Labs’ Rumalla said several signers could still authorize a malicious transaction if they were all deceived by the same compromised interface.
Related: Can crypto users trust the supply chain behind hardware wallets?
Tangem says its seedless design simplifies self-custody by removing the need to manage a recovery phrase. Users must instead safeguard the physical devices that provide access to their funds.
A private key is generated on one card, with backup copies stored on up to two additional devices. Tangem confirmed to Cointelegraph that losing every device would permanently lock users out of their funds.
The company said it had received no reports of users losing all their cards.
Keeping the cards safe also does not protect users from approving a malicious transaction. Zach Herbert, CEO of rival hardware wallet maker Foundation, said seedless backups can preserve self-custody, but criticized Tangem’s lack of a built-in screen, which leaves users relying on their smartphones to verify transaction details.
“An attacker does not need to extract your private key if they can trick you into authorizing a transaction that empties your wallet,” he said.

title: BTC news: Bitcoin will now stop hiding bugs an AI can find in one prompt
text:
Bitcoin Core, the software most of the bitcoin network runs on, will stop sitting on bug fixes for months when the bug is one an AI could find again, after its maintainers merged a change to the project’s security policy on Thursday.
Core previously graded every reported vulnerability by severity and timed disclosure accordingly. Low-severity flaws were revealed two weeks after the next major version shipped. Medium and high ones stayed under embargo until two weeks after the last affected version reached end of life.
The logic was that shipping a fix quietly and explaining it much later kept attackers from learning about a hole before the people running nodes, the computers that check and relay every bitcoin transaction, had upgraded.
But the old rule was built for a world where finding a bug took skill, and the spread of AI tools has broken how that process worked.
“We recently experienced an increase in the number of reports for security vulnerabilities that can be easily (re-)discovered,” Antoine Poinsot, the Chaincode Labs developer who wrote the change, said in his proposal.
“This is largely due to LLMs drastically reducing the bar to find certain classes of issues or identify covert fixes.”
Core can now flag a bug as easy to discover during triage, which in practice means one that “can be found with a simple prompt to an LLM.” Those bugs get a fix copied back to every version Core still supports, shipped in a point release “as soon as possible” along with a security advisory carrying some details.
“For these issues that are easy to find, this is the wrong tradeoff,” the policy reads of the old embargo. “The embargo period achieves little but it delays the availability of a fixed release.”
Fixes “won’t have as much ‘bake time’” in testing before they reach users, however, Poinsot wrote.
Not every developer agreed on how far to go. Antoine Riard, a longtime bitcoin security researcher, wanted Core to keep the option of shipping a fix without an advisory and holding the details back case by case.
Poinsot refused. “Alerting users of a security vulnerability without any details could create more risk unnecessarily,” he wrote, pointing to “a rushed migration by users who would otherwise not be affected.”
A volunteer group of 16 developers calling itself the Bitcoin Red Team ran AI models across 390 bitcoin projects in about a day in late July and logged 4,962 findings, with 85 of them critical.
Within days a BTCPay Server flaw the group had reported privately was being exploited on live merchant servers. The attacks drained the Lightning nodes merchants use to take small bitcoin payments. Core Lightning, one of the main Lightning implementations, told operators to disconnect after AI-generated reports to its small team turned out to be real.
A bigger loss came from a bug no AI needed to find. A flaw in Coldcard hardware-wallet firmware, dormant since 2021, let attackers drain 594 BTC in 25 minutes on July 30, and losses neared $114 million across four sweeps. When Coldcard shipped its fix, it said AI had helped catch more bugs along the way.
No bug has been flagged under the new rule yet, but a secret any model can regenerate in one prompt was never going to protect users for long.

title: Heatbit's $899 Water Heater Element Mines Bitcoin While It Heats Your Tank - Decrypt
text:
Heatbit, which makes space heaters with built-in Bitcoin miners, has unveiled a water heater element that mines Bitcoin while it heats water, the company said in a tweet on Thursday.
The element, called Bitwater, replaces the resistance wire in a standard electric water heater element with 20 Bitcoin mining chips, so the heat they give off warms the water instead. "Same heat, same electricity, plus bitcoin," Heatbit wrote, arguing that "the electricity was going to be spent on hot water anyway."
Introducing Bitwater: the water heater element that mines Bitcoin.
It screws into the electric tank you already have.
Physically decentralized mining that runs no matter what 🧵
Heat water. Mine Bitcoin. Same tank. pic.twitter.com/pRdxPbmpXM
— Heatbit (@heatbit_com) October 22, 2026
The element uses 20 of Bitmain's BM1370 chips and is rated at up to 34 terahashes per second, drawing up to 600 watts at an efficiency of 12 joules per terahash. The water cools the chips, so there are no fans and no noise, according to the company.
Heatbit describes installation as a do-it-yourself job: switch off the breaker, drain the tank, unscrew the old element and thread in Bitwater using an included wrench. It fits the standard one-inch port on regular 30- to 80-gallon electric tanks in the U.S. and Canada, including those made by A. O. Smith, Rheem, Bradford White, Whirlpool and GE, Heatbit said in a follow-up tweet, with no plumbing changes or new circuit needed.
At up to 600 watts, Bitwater draws far less power than the 4,500-watt elements common in U.S. tanks. Those heat water fast and then shut off, while Bitwater heats more slowly and runs for longer, Heatbit explained. When demand spikes, the tank's existing upper element still provides backup.
Users can track water temperature, hashrate and earnings in an app and choose between solo mining and joining a pool, with mined Bitcoin going to an address they control.
Preorders for the first production run, which Heatbit calls its "Genesis batch," cost $899, with later batches priced at up to $1,299. The refundable preorders are due to ship in the first quarter of 2027. Heatbit said it tested the element through the winter with households of four and five in New York and Florida, and teased a product for homes with gas water heaters.
Heatbit has not published its own earnings estimate. Instead, it shared a reply from xAI's Grok chatbot putting earnings at about $1 to $1.25 a day, adding that "estimates aren't guarantees." That is in line with Decrypt's own figures. At the current hashprice of about $36.73 per petahash per second per day, according to Hashrate Index, an element running at its full 34 TH/s would mine about $1.25 worth of Bitcoin a day, or roughly $455 a year. Heatbit says the element is built to run more than 80% of the time, and earnings would rise and fall with Bitcoin's price and network difficulty.
Heatbit is pitching Bitwater as a way to spread Bitcoin mining across homes. Homes worldwide use about 300 terawatt-hours of electricity a year heating water, compared with about 170 terawatt-hours for the entire Bitcoin network, the company said.
"Public miners are fleeing to AI and dumping coins to pay Wall Street and CEO salaries," Heatbit wrote. "Home miners answer to no one."
Large public miners have been moving into AI. Bitcoin miners struck 17 deals worth more than $110 billion over two years, contracting out roughly 6 gigawatts of power to companies including Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Nvidia and CoreWeave, Bernstein said earlier this year. The bank expects AI revenue at the miners it covers to grow from $1.2 billion in 2026 to $10.7 billion by 2030, and has said the sector's planned power capacity of more than 27 gigawatts makes miners key suppliers for the AI boom.
The two businesses work differently, though. Bitcoin miners can switch off to relieve pressure on the grid, while AI data centers need power around the clock. "We're interruptible [as Bitcoin miners], whereas a traditional data center needs (to be) on 100% of the time," Shanon Squires of Compass Mining told Decrypt in March 2025.
The company's first product, a space heater with a built-in miner, cost almost $700 in 2023. Founder Alex Busarov told Decrypt at the time that it would always earn something however mining economics changed, because the heat it produced was replacing a conventional heater's. "Dyson doesn't make you any money. This one does," he said.

title: Cysic Hacker Sends $744K to Tornado Cash After 10% Bounty Offer
text:
The attacker moved $744,000 in ETH and BNB to Tornado Cash after exploiting Cysic’s bridge to mint 10 million tokens on BNB Smart Chain.
The wallet linked to the Cysic bridge exploit sent about $744,000 in cryptocurrencies to Tornado Cash on Friday after the Cysic Foundation offered the attacker a 10% recovery bounty.
The address transferred 300 Ether (ETH) and 30.4 BNB to the crypto mixer, according to blockchain security company PeckShield.
The hacker exploited a bridge vulnerability to mint 10 million Cysic (CYS) tokens on BNB Smart Chain on Saturday. Cysic suspended the bridge and blacklisted the recipient address, freezing about 2.8 million of the newly minted tokens. The foundation said its mainnet and existing assets in user wallets were unaffected.
The following Thursday, the Cysic Foundation offered the hacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning 275.872 ETH, worth about $665,000, representing roughly 90% of the identified Ether proceeds.
Tornado Cash pools deposits from multiple addresses, making the funds harder to trace. The attacker’s Ethereum wallet held just $45 in ETH at press time, according to Akham data.
Cointelegraph contacted the Cysic Foundation for comment on fund recovery efforts but did not receive a response by publication.

title: Uniswap's aggregator hooks go live on Ethereum, Base and Robinhood Chain
text: Uniswap Labs has launched aggregator hooks on Ethereum, Base and Robinhood Chain, allowing Uniswap v4 to route trades through liquidity held on external platforms. Fluid, Curve and PancakeSwap are among the external sources available at launch, Uniswap Labs said Thursday. The hooks are available through the Uniswap web app and API, with support for more blockchains planned. The first aggregator hook went live in March 2026 on Tempo, a payments-focused blockchain developed by Stripe and Paradigm. Tempo is supported only through the web app, while Ethereum, Base and Robinhood Chain are supported through both Uniswap's web app and API, a Uniswap Labs spokesperson told The Block. Uniswap first introduced plans for aggregator hooks in its UNIfication proposal in November 2025. The company described the update as turning v4 into an aggregator. How aggregator hooks work Hooks are a feature of Uniswap v4 that let developers add custom rules and functions to liquidity pools. Aggregator hooks make liquidity on other platforms look like a Uniswap v4 pool. Uniswap compares prices across its own pools and other platforms, then completes the trade in one transaction. "Each Aggregator Hook wraps an external source in a Uniswap v4 hook, so that any router sees it as a Uniswap pool," Uniswap Labs said. The external sources will be included automatically when users swap through the Uniswap web app. Developers using the Uniswap API can also route trades through the hooks. Protocol fees and UNI token burns Trades routed through external liquidity sources will pay Uniswap protocol fees, according to Uniswap Labs. Those fees will contribute to UNI token burns. Uniswap Labs said the protocol has processed more than $4.5 trillion in total trading volume. While most onchain liquidity is already available on Uniswap, liquidity can still form elsewhere, it said, adding that aggregator hooks are designed to bring those sources into v4. title: Bitcoin (BTC) price volatility is well above euro-dollar's, though it has calmed down: Crypto Daily
Bitcoin in 'Wait and See Mode'—And That Might Be a Good Thing - Decrypt
text:
Bitcoin hasn't budged more than 6% over the past month, per Decrypt data, and is currently sitting at around $81,735, down 1.2% on the day. One expert says the leading cryptocurrency is in "wait and see mode," and claims that might be a good thing.
The crypto market as a whole has been quiet lately. Every top five cryptocurrency has failed to move more than 2% over the past week. And the Crypto Fear and Greed Index is at a neutral score of 47. It's all quite… boring.
But market analysts say that a dull market might actually portend a bull market, and that there are still opportunities out there.
A quiet market is "usually a good sign, and one reason is that it doesn't last," Jake Koch-Gallup, senior research analyst at Blockworks, told Decrypt. "In the past, similar low-volatility stretches have led to 30% price swings in either direction within a few months."
André Dragosch, head of research at Bitwise Europe, called the quiet period a "constructive sign." That's because "long stretches of uneventful trading punctuated by a handful of outsized moves" is a typical early sign of a bull market.
The drawdowns in Bitcoin's current recovery have also been less damaging than in previous cycles, Dragosch said. That's all while oil, semiconductor stocks, and government bonds are experiencing "elevated" volatility, he added.
"That tells us investors are increasingly willing to absorb weakness and maintain exposure," Dragosch told Decrypt, calling it "resilience rather than euphoria."
Conversely, Carlos Guzman, vice president of research at crypto trading firm GSR, told Decrypt that a boring market isn't either a good or a bad sign. Rather, he said, the market is standing still due to a "risk-off" sentiment taking over global markets.
"This has been mostly due to factors outside of crypto, with a complex macro situation and fears around AI stocks taking center stage," Guzman said. "We're unlikely to see a significant market breakout while broader risk-off sentiment prevails, so markets continue to be choppy."
Dragosch told Decrypt that Bitcoin is in "wait and see mode," with markets stuck between tightening global financial conditions and an expectation that slowing growth will eventually force central banks to change course.
Mostly, what Bitcoin is waiting for is the Federal Reserve. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, and CPI then rose 0.6% for September. The Fed's next rate decision is on October 28, "and until then nobody wants to make a big bet," Koch-Gallup said.
Bitcoin is hovering around what Dragosch calls "the market's economic midpoint," the level where roughly half of all invested capital is in profit and half is at a loss. That means "neither buyers nor sellers currently have much incentive to move the market away from this level," he said.
That doesn't mean nobody is buying. Bitcoin briefly dipped below $80,000 last week but "quickly found buyers," Guzman said, and BlackRock's Bitcoin ETF saw an inflow of $665.20 million on Monday, according to CoinGlass data.
"The problem is that buying hasn't been consistent enough to drive a sustained rally," Guzman said.
Koch-Gallup said three catalysts are coming in the next two weeks: the Fed decision on October 28, an options expiry on October 30 of $11.69 billion worth of Bitcoin, and the U.S. midterms on November 3. These events could dictate the crypto market's next major move.
"If the Fed keeps rates the same and ETF inflows keep coming, I'd expect the break to be upward," Koch-Gallup said. "If the Fed hikes again, the $75,000 to $77,000 floor comes back into play."
Plus, Guzman added that a resolution to tensions around the Strait of Hormuz could also act as a catalyst for markets.
Dragosch said derivatives markets are pricing in far less volatility than on-chain data suggests, which means options are "unusually cheap right now, both for hedging and for positioning for a larger move in either direction."
"For me, a boring market is the time to buy high-quality protocols before a bull market makes them overvalued," Koch-Gallup told Decrypt. "I'm focused on revenue-generating businesses with strong tokenholder claims."
While Bitcoin and other major tokens have traded sideways, smaller coins have made moves.
Brave browser token BAT has climbed almost 87% to a $263 million market cap over the past month, according to Decrypt data, while card collection marketplace Collector Crypt has jumped 95% to $318 million.
"A boring market means you have to work harder to find the opportunities, not that they aren't there," Koch-Gallup said.

title: Bybit Secures First Full Dubai Spot Trading Licence
text:
Bybit’s new VARA licence authorizes spot trading services in Dubai, but the exchange must complete additional regulatory requirements before launching.
Crypto exchange Bybit has secured a full Dubai license for spot trading following its earlier in-principle approval.
Bybit said Thursday that its Dubai entity, Bybit Fintech FZE, received a virtual asset service provider (VASP) license from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA) for exchange services, including spot trading.
A Bybit spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the entity’s previous in-principle approval was non-operational and did not permit it to serve customers in Dubai. VARA’s public register lists the new license as active, allowing services to retail, qualified and institutional investors.
The spokesperson said Bybit must still complete VARA’s launch process and meet operational requirements before starting spot trading services. The company did not provide a launch date.
Bybit previously secured a full Virtual Asset Platform Operator license from the United Arab Emirates’ federal regulator, the Securities and Commodities Authority (SCA), in October 2025. However, the exchange’s service restrictions exclude Dubai from the jurisdictions served by its SCA-licensed entity, Bybit Virtual Asset Platform Operator LLC.
The spokesperson declined to comment on how the VARA license differs from the SCA approval or whether the earlier license permitted services in Dubai.

title: Live updates: Bitcoin holds above $81,000 as oil prices hit six-month high
text:
“This part of October is historically one of the worst of the year,” writes Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group.
“The good news is late October lows are quite normal and with sentiment getting extreme, we could be looking at another late October buying period.”
Detrick is writing about traditional equity markets, but to the extent that crypto markets are correlated, it’s worth considering.
Yesterday’s 19 basis point slide in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was the largest one-day move downward since March 2023, when the failure of Silicon Valley Bank had investors worried about a domino effect across the country.
Markets having calmed for the moment — the Nasdaq and S&P 500 are about flat on Friday, and French bond spreads (to Germany) are little changed — yields are cautiously edging higher.
The U.S. 10-year yield is up 4.3 basis points to 4.994%, and the 2-year yield is up 6 basis points to 4.695%.
Next week brings the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting, and investors continue to overwhelmingly bet the central bank leaves its benchmark fed funds rate unchanged.
Gold fell below $4,000 an ounce for the first time since July, trading around $3,990, roughly 30% below its January all-time high of $5,600. Silver has dropped more than 2% over the past 24 hours to around $53.40 an ounce, leaving it 56% below its January record high.
Brent crude oil — typically considered the global benchmark — is now higher by 2.6% and above $116 per barrel for the first time since late April
WTI crude oil — the U.S. domestic benchmark, is ahead 3.1% to a one-month higher of $102.53.
U.S. stocks are modestly lower, the Nasdaq down 0.2% and the S&P 500 off 0.6%.
Bitcoin has turned lower too, dipping back to $81,000.
The University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment edged down to 48.0 in October from 48.1 a month earlier. That’s up, though, from the preliminary reading of 46.3 two weeks ago.
The Index of Consumer Expectations rose to 48.8 from 46.3.
One-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7% from 4.6%, but were flat from the 4.7% preliminary read.
Longer-run inflation expectations rose to 3.5% from 3.4%, also in line with the preliminary read.
Good news is bad news as the AI trade continues to struggle. Bloom Energy (BE) shares fell 10% in U.S. trading on Friday despite beating revenue and earnings expectations on Thursday. Third-quarter revenue rose 138% year over year to $1.24 billion, exceeding forecasts of $1.07 billion, while adjusted earnings per share reached $0.94, ahead of the $0.67 expected.
Even with yesterday’s ugly action included, bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 has gained about 39% over the nearly four months since it sat just below $59,000 on July 1.
One trader crunched the numbers. Since July 1, there have been 2,724 hourly candles, and the 15 strongest candles — just 0.55% — produced enough gains for that entire 39% advance.
Removing the 20 strongest hours over the last four months, and bitcoin would have actually dropped 6.8%.
“This is exactly why going fully cash and waiting for the ‘perfect entry’ is so dangerous,” the trader concluded. “Bitcoin could spend weeks doing absolutely nothing and deliver the entire rally while you are waiting to buy lower.”
Bitcoin continues to struggle below the average cost basis of U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs, trading just above $81,000 compared with $82,313.
The chart tracks the running average price at which bitcoin has flowed into these ETFs.
The U.S.-listed spot bitcoin ETF suffered $635 million in outflows during yesterday’s panicky action, according to Farside Investors. That’s the largest daily outflow since June 25.
While the contrarian take might be, “fantastic, the leveraged, fast-money types were flushed out, and now we’re poised to move higher,” history suggests otherwise.
According to Farside, bitcoin has tended to perform poorly in the days and weeks following outsized outflows. For instances of outflows greater than $300 million (there have been 22 such days prior to yesterday), bitcoin, on average, was significantly lower 7, 30, and 90 days later.
The caveat, of course, is that history is quite limited, given the ETFs have been around for less than three years, and is also likely skewed by the bear market begun in October 2025.
Bitcoin dipped to about $81,000 late Thursday and has since spent the day boxed in a range of less than $1,000, trading near $81,500 early Friday. After a week of $3,000 swings, it’s the calmest stretch bitcoin has had in days.
It’s down 0.4% over 24 hours and still sits below $82,500, the support it lost on Thursday.
Altcoins were mixed. BNB was the standout, up nearly 2% to about $745, and DOGE added about 1%. XMR gave back part of Thursday’s jump, falling 7% to about $607, and ZEC lost nearly 4% to about $1,200. HYPE, XRP, ether and SOL slipped about 1% or less, with ether just under $2,400, according to CoinDesk data.
Stocks found their footing too. Nasdaq 100 futures were little changed after the index’s worst day since June, and an ETF tracking chipmakers edged higher before the open. Meta kept falling, while SpaceX climbed on reports that it plans to become a wireless carrier.
Oil is the worry. Brent crude touched its highest level since early May, which complicates the inflation outlook heading into the Fed’s Oct. 27–28 meeting. Treasuries gave back some of Thursday’s haven rally, which had pushed the 10-year yield down by the most in more than a year. Gold and the dollar were flat.

title: Is the Internet Safe Again After the PHP Nightmare? What You Need to Know - Decrypt
text:
A day after two bugs in PHP sent governments scrambling to unplug their websites, the fix is out, attackers are hammering away, and a lot of people are asking the same thing: Can I use the internet without worrying, or should I hide under the bed until next week?
The short answer is that the internet didn't break, and for most people the risk sits with the websites they visit, not with their own phones or laptops. The longer answer has a few caveats worth knowing.
Quick recap: PHP is the software that runs behind the scenes on about 70% of websites whose server-side language is known, and the two flaws, nicknamed PHP2Shell, let a stranger take control of a vulnerable server without logging in.
So, is the exploit fixed? Yes, mostly. PHP released versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 on Wednesday, according to its release notes. "There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice." As of Thursday, PHP has not issued any follow-up patch.
A fix only helps once someone installs it, though. PHP doesn't update itself, so every hosting company, IT department, and solo website owner has to apply it on their own servers, and then restart the software for it to take effect.
In other words, the fix is out there, but it doesn’t mean the sites you visit are necessarily safe.
PHP 8.1 and earlier no longer get official releases, which makes older servers the weak spot, although PHP's security team posted bare-bones patches for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1 for people who compile the software themselves.
Attackers certainly tried: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said his network saw thousands of exploit attempts in the 10 hours before the announcement, tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after it, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions since.
Some stats on #php2shell. In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the @Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it. That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.
— Matthew Prince 🌥 (@eastdakota) October 22, 2026
Amazon went further, saying its decoy servers logged an attempt on October 17, four days before the bugs went public. "It remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure," Amazon CISO CJ Moses wrote, adding that PHP2Shell is "now being broadly exploited in the wild."
Governments, however, don’t seem to have experienced any sort of successful break-in yet. Thomas Caspers, vice president of Germany's federal cybersecurity agency BSI, said the agency had seen attacks but no successful use of the flaws, adding: "It seems a little bit more complicated than expected to exploit." Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary, Minoru Kihara, also said no attacks exploiting the flaws had been confirmed.
An attempt is someone rattling the doorknob; a breach is someone getting inside, so both claims can be true at once. Millions of rattled doorknobs and zero confirmed break-ins is good news, but break-ins tend to be discovered later, not in real time.
It sort of was. In a blog post published Wednesday, the PHP Foundation said its security work in 2024 "found the first signs of the OOM problem behind CVE-2026-109618," meaning the out-of-memory bug at the heart of one of the two flaws.
The team came up with "several competing approaches" to fix it but "struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice," according to the foundation. "Without the Foundation's funding it would have been impossible to have multiple people work on this issue full time," it added.
"We won't pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources," the foundation wrote, adding that its security team, which used to need consensus, will now decide by majority. For the software running most of the web, that security work "still depends on a small group of foundation-funded developers and a little volunteer help," per the post.
Because patching takes time, and "offline" was the official advice for anyone who couldn't patch right away. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre told organizations to consider "taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated."
The list of sites that went dark on Wednesday got long fast. According to TechRadar, it included Wikimedia services, Orange websites and apps across dozens of countries, 32 UK government services, Dutch hospitals, and Germany's federal IT provider, ITZBund.
The UK's Office for Budget Responsibility and Edinburgh's council website were back by Thursday. Others, like the Dutch anonymous crime-reporting site Meld Misdaad Anoniem, were still offline Thursday morning, according to DutchNews.
Not because of this, at least not yet. No confirmed data breach has been tied to PHP2Shell so far, and changing every password today won't help if a site's server is still unpatched.
What does help is the boring stuff: unique passwords for every account, two-factor authentication turned on, and paying attention if a company emails you about a breach in the coming weeks. If one shows up, change that password, and any account where you reused it.
Website owners have more homework, because patching closes the door but doesn't tell you whether someone walked in first. Security firm Tag1 advises looking for PHP files you didn't upload, new scheduled tasks, and new accounts, and rotating database passwords and API keys on any internet-facing server that ran a vulnerable version.
Binance founder Changpeng Zhao had a short piece of advice on X: "Call me paranoid, but be extra careful visiting ANY web site in the next few days."
Call me paranoid, but be extra careful visiting ANY web site in the next few days, as some web admins are not always up-to-date with security patches.
Two vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) reported for PHP, the web programming language, affecting servers…
— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) October 21, 2026
A hacked web server can show you a fake version of a real site, and in crypto that usually means a page that asks you to connect your wallet and approve a transaction that empties it. A blockchain network itself may be fine; the websites in front of it might not be.
For the next few days, triple-check what you're signing, bookmark the sites you use instead of clicking links, and use a hardware wallet if you have one. So far, no crypto exchange has publicly reported a breach tied to PHP2Shell.
Browsing the web today is about as safe as it was last week, which is to say not perfectly. The real exposure is on servers that haven't been patched, and security company Mallory counted roughly 884,000 internet-facing hosts running PHP versions that get no official fix.
Amazon's advice to defenders is basically that this isn’t over. "Defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation." Any server that ran a vulnerable version since at least October 17 should be checked, not just patched.

title: HSBC Launches RedCoin Stablecoin for Hong Kong Payments
text:
HSBC is rolling out RedCoin wallets to PayMe users, with plans to support tokenized investment subscriptions and expand into institutional uses.
HSBC has launched its first Hong Kong-dollar stablecoin, RedCoin (RCHKD), for transfers and merchant payments through its PayMe app.
More than 3.3 million PayMe users will be able to activate stablecoin wallets in the app in the coming days, the bank announced Friday.
RedCoin is designed to be redeemable one-for-one for Hong Kong dollars. HSBC Digital Assets Custody provides safekeeping services for the stablecoin.
The consumer rollout follows Anchorpoint’s rollout of its HKDAP stablecoin through HashKey Exchange in August, which initially targeted eligible institutions and professional investors.
HSBC received its stablecoin issuer license in April, alongside Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture backed by Standard Chartered, Animoca Brands and HKT. The two were the first companies approved under Hong Kong’s stablecoin regulatory framework.
The bank said it plans to introduce RedCoin wallets to its HSBC HK Mobile Banking App later this year, allowing customers to subscribe to tokenized investment products, including a new share class of its Hong Kong dollar money market fund.
HSBC also plans to expand RedCoin into wholesale corporate and institutional applications.

ChatGPT Teaches Messi Chess—On a Board It Set Up Wrong, With an Opening That Loses in Four Moves - Decrypt
text:
Lionel Messi posted an ad on Instagram on Wednesday in which ChatGPT teaches him chess. The trillion-dollar chatbot flubbed the lesson so hard, Chess-knowing commentators online are losing it.
The digital board on screen in the ad has each side’s king and queen swapped, and OpenAI's chatbot recommends Messi open it up with a move that is almost guaranteed to lose in four turns.
The post, from the second most-followed person on the platform with more than 517 million followers, collected roughly 1.9 million likes and 19,600 comments in about a day.
OpenAI says more than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT every week, and its latest pitch to them is one of the most famous athletes alive getting a chess lesson from a tutor that cannot set up the board.
If the thing sold as your all-knowing teacher fumbles move zero, it’s fair to wonder what else it delivers with a straight face.
In the post, Messi says he asked ChatGPT “to teach me a chess opening that matched my style,” and the chatbot suggested the “GOAT Horns,” a pun on the nickname Messi has carried for years. (GOAT stands for greatest of all time, for those who don’t follow sports lingo.)
Messi, of course, is known for winning games—not losing them in record time.
An opening is just the first few moves of a game. Magnus Carlsen, the world’s top-ranked player and arguably the best player in the history of the game, has played this opening, but he is also the man who played the Bongcloud—a joke opening that drags the king out on move two—against Hikaru Nakamura in 2021, so copying what Carlsen does for fun is not exactly a beginner’s syllabus.
In real chess each queen starts on a square of her own color with the king beside her, and in the ad both armies have those two pieces trading places.
The swap is not just cosmetic, because the Goat Horns moves played from that setup hand White’s queen a clear diagonal that ends up on a check mate on move four against Black—as fast as the Scholar’s mate, the fastest way to lose in Chess.
On a correct board the same moves produce no forced mate.
Reddit noticed. “How did no one like, oh I don't know, look at this for less than 5 seconds before sending it to the whole world?” pseudonymous user Cannonheim asked.
Another wrote: “Two options, either they are idiots or they are too clever, which is exactly why people are talking about it,” another one mused. A third user argued that maybe this whole thing was the fault of some random intern.
Messi asked ChatGPT to teach him a chess opening that matched his style. It suggested Goat Horns 🤘 pic.twitter.com/7w25w8LEZP
— ChatGPT (@ChatGPT) October 22, 2026
Users on r/chess said an earlier OpenAI ad had already made the same mistake, putting Black’s queen on e8 instead of d8, and one commenter wrote: “Nearly a trillion dollar evaluation and they can’t put the queen on the right square lol.”
The ad landed exactly two weeks after OpenAI rolled out GPT-6 with Intelligent UI, a feature that lets ChatGPT answer with interactive charts, buttons, and forms instead of plain text. Messi’s marketing deal with OpenAI started in June, when he posted an image made with ChatGPT Images ahead of the World Cup.
ChatGPT isn’t exactly Stockfish. Back in 2025, ChatGPT lost the final of a chatbot chess tournament, hosted by International Master Levy Rozman, after making illegal moves such as promoting pawns that did not exist but spawned out of thin air.
Thankfully, OpenAI fixed it in post and changed the pieces in a separate ad for X. The pieces are OK, the opening is still horrible to play, especially for a beginner like Messi.
The original video is still live on Messi’s Instagram.

title: Malaysia, Thailand Join Singapore’s BLOOM Digital Money Initiative
text:
BLOOM seeks to cut costs by helping financial institutions coordinate cross-border use of stablecoins and tokenized deposits.
Bank Negara Malaysia and the Bank of Thailand joined Singapore’s BLOOM initiative on Friday as policymaker members.
BLOOM, short for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency, is a public-private initiative that intends to help financial institutions use stablecoins and tokenized deposits for cross-border payments.
According to the Monetary Authority of Singapore, BLOOM aims to cut costs and help institutions bring services to market faster by reducing the need for institutions to set up arrangements with each counterparty or market.
MAS launched BLOOM in October 2025, building on Project Orchid, which began in 2021 to explore uses for a digital Singapore dollar. BLOOM’s work also covers corporate cash management, trade finance and payments executed by AI agents within predefined limits.
BLOOM’s participants include Airwallex, Mastercard, Ripple, Visa and the World Bank Group.
Bank Negara Malaysia separately announced in February that three initiatives would test ringgit stablecoins and tokenized deposits for domestic and cross-border wholesale payments in 2026.

title: a16z Drops Crypto From Its Name, Widens Bets to AI and Frontier Tech - Decrypt
text:
Andreessen Horowitz, the venture capital firm better known as a16z, is renaming its crypto fund “a16z Frontier” and widening its mandate to AI and other emerging technologies, according to an email shared with its newsletter subscribers on Thursday.
a16z is among the biggest backers of the crypto industry, and when a firm that size drops “crypto” from its name, it shows where it may expect the next wave of cash to go. Chris Dixon, a general partner who runs the crypto team, says the firm’s bets include Coinbase, the blockchain network Solana, and Uniswap, a platform where people swap tokens without a middleman.
a16z calls the move “an expansion” and says crypto stays: “we will continue to invest in crypto and related ventures and advocate for sensible crypto regulation,” the firm wrote.
The argument is that blockchains—shared digital ledgers that record who owns what without a bank in the middle—have faded into the background of products people already use.
“Wall Street and fintech companies now regularly launch products built on blockchains. Does that make them crypto companies? The label matters less now,” Dixon wrote, adding that it makes more sense to define companies “by what they do rather than by the technologies they use.”
In January, a16z said it had raised more than $15 billion across its funds, and co-founder Ben Horowitz wrote in a firm post that the mission “starts with winning the key architectures of the future—AI and crypto.”
Dixon expects more “native use cases,” which he defines as “brand-new activities you couldn’t do before,” since AI so far has mostly made existing work like coding “faster, better, and cheaper.” Early versions, he says, “will look strange and unserious, like toys and hobbies,” before some grow into mainstream products.
The new label covers startups “building new technologies and creating markets that may take years to develop,” a bet Dixon says goes back more than a decade.
“When I joined a16z in 2013, I made these kinds of long-horizon investments a focus,” Dixon wrote. “The growth of smartphones made cameras, sensors, and chips better and cheaper, enabling new devices like drones, AR/VR headsets, and wearables. That theme led to investments in Oculus and drone startups like Skydio and Zipline.”
The next wave, he says, includes “autonomous machines that can perceive, reason, and act in the physical world” as well as advances in biology and medicine.
He also envisions a post-AGI society referring to artificial general intelligence, a still-theoretical AI that can match or beat humans at nearly all thinking tasks.
Crypto stays in the picture because Dixon sees it giving AI agents, meaning programs that act on their own, a way to pay each other. “Crypto can give new networks native economic capabilities, enable machine-to-machine transactions, and create new ways to bootstrap them,” he wrote.
Dixon made a similar argument in 2022, when crypto’s total market value had fallen about two-thirds from its 2021 peak. “What I look at is not prices,” he said then, pointing to developer and entrepreneur activity as the core metric.
Dixon will lead the new fund alongside a16z founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz and general partners Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet. His post gives no size for the renamed fund, so the latest figure on record is the $2.2 billion announced in May.

title: Bitcoin ETFs Lose $635M as October Flows Turn Negative
text:
Thursday’s withdrawals ended a three-day inflow streak and left US spot Bitcoin ETFs with $175 million in net outflows for October.
US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded $635 million in net outflows on Thursday, pushing October’s flows back into the red.
The withdrawals more than erased Wednesday’s $528 million in inflows and brought October’s net outflows to $175 million, according to SoSoValue data.
It was the largest single-day net outflow since June 25, when Bitcoin ETFs lost $696 million. The withdrawals snapped a three-day inflow streak that attracted $1.08 billion.
Bitcoin ETFs still had weekly net inflows of $443 million. The funds had recorded two consecutive weeks of outflows before the rebound.
Bitcoin traded between $80,996 and $82,551 on Thursday, down from Wednesday’s intraday high of $84,777. BTC was trading at approximately $81,783 at the time of publication, down around 1% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko.
Altcoin ETFs also saw mostly negative flows on Thursday. Ether ETFs recorded around $111 million in net outflows, followed by Solana ETFs with roughly $9 million and Hyperliquid (HYPE) ETFs with about $8 million. XRP ETFs bucked the trend, attracting around $3.6 million in inflows.

Meta Creates Non-Voting Stock to Fund AI Buildout, Keeping Zuckerberg in Control - Decrypt
text:
Meta's board has approved a new class of non-voting stock, and every holder of Class A and Class B shares will receive one new share for each share they own. The company disclosed the plan on Wednesday with its third-quarter results, and the Class C shares come into existence on Jan. 19, 2027.
The one-for-one dividend works as a two-for-one stock split, and Meta says it will not change anyone's voting power. Because Class C shares generally carry no vote, Meta can sell them for cash, or use them as pay and acquisition currency, without shrinking Mark Zuckerberg's control.
Zuckerberg held about 60.6% of the voting power on Oct. 1 against a 13.4% economic interest, according to the information statement Meta filed with the SEC. The gap comes from the dual-class setup, where Class A shares carry one vote each and Class B shares carry 10, and he beneficially owns about 341 million Class B shares.
According to the SEC filing, advisers at Moelis told the board's special committee that Meta could raise about $700 billion in equity over several years before Zuckerberg's voting power fell below 50%, according to the filing. Management also told those advisers that its long-term forecasts showed a need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several years, starting as early as fall 2026.
CFO Susan Li framed the filing's "hundreds of billions" language differently on a follow-up call with analysts, calling it "a theoretical maximum" computed to determine what level of equity financing would trigger a loss of founder control. It is "not actually a description of our present equity financing needs or plans," she said, and Meta does not have "anything to announce on that front." The structure is approved, while the size and timing of any equity sale are not disclosed.
Under a Founder Alignment Agreement signed Oct. 20, only 20% of the Class C shares Zuckerberg receives can be sold freely. Selling any of the other 80% generally requires him to sell or convert a matching Class A or Class B share within two business days, which trims his voting power.
The agreement also commits Zuckerberg to remain a California resident, or live wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years. The filing says California's Proposition 40, a wealth tax on the Nov. 3 ballot, could make him liable for a multi-billion dollar payment, and that Zuckerberg stated selling Class B shares to cover it could cut his voting interest to about 53%.
The board has also agreed to pay another one-for-one Class C dividend each time the 30-day volume-weighted average price of Class C reaches a successive doubling of the $580.60 Class A price from Sept. 10, adjusted for splits, as long as shareholder returns compound at 10% or more a year.
Class C shares are identical to Class A and Class B except for voting rights, but the filing warns they will likely trade at some discount to Class A, and Meta may need to issue more of them for any equity sale. Class C also will not count as "voting stock" under Section 368(a) of the tax code, so sellers who want to defer taxes on a deal may push for a different structure.
Meta's board had not set the record or payment dates for the dividend as of its filing, and the payment must come within five business days after the charter takes effect on Jan. 19, 2027.

title: Ethereum Delays Glamsterdam Upgrade After Security Researchers Flag Risks
text:
ChainSecurity said it identified 13 real-world examples of smart contracts potentially affected by Glamsterdam’s gas changes and is coordinating responsible disclosure with affected projects.
Ethereum developers have postponed the Glamsterdam hard fork on the Hoodi testnet after researchers identified gas-related security risks that could affect how existing smart contracts handle failed transactions.
The Ethereum Foundation (EF) said that the upgrade, originally scheduled for Oct. 26, would be delayed to allow developers to investigate how some proposals interact with smart contracts deployed on Ethereum.
On Oct. 13, Blockchain security firm ChainSecurity warned that two proposals included in Glamsterdam, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, could weaken safeguards against a type of attack called insufficient gas griefing.
The postponement raises uncertainty over Glamsterdam’s mainnet timeline. Ethereum developers had been considering early December, with plans to finalize a schedule following successful Hoodi testing.
In its analysis, ChainSecurity said that under the new rules, gas could be returned to a contract after an operation fails, allowing it to continue running when it previously would have stopped. The researchers said the changes could interfere with existing security checks that rely on how much gas remains available during a transaction.
In attacks known as insufficient gas griefing, a malicious caller deliberately provides too little gas for a legitimate smart contract operation to succeed. ChainSecurity warned that Glamsterdam’s proposed changes could undermine safeguards against such attacks, potentially allowing contracts to permanently record failed operations.
For example, an affected contract could remove a user’s claim or disable the option to retry it, leaving the user unable to complete an otherwise valid operation.
ChainSecurity said Glamsterdam would not make all gas-related security checks unreliable. Some safeguards could still work, but developers would need to review them to ensure they account for the upgrade’s new gas rules.
Related: Ethereum Foundation warns some tools may break with Glamsterdam upgrade
The findings prompted concern among Ethereum contributors. In an Oct. 21 comment on GitHub, pseudonymous security researcher pcaversaccio described the risks as “serious” and called for a reassessment of the hard fork.
On Friday, ChainSecurity said it had identified “13 real-world examples” and was coordinating responsible disclosure with affected projects. The security firm did not disclose details of the 13 real-world examples or identify the affected projects. However, the company said developers should check their contracts as soon as possible.
The findings follow an earlier Ethereum Foundation warning that Glamsterdam’s gas model could break wallets, indexers, and gas estimators that rely on fixed assumptions. The upgrade was previously activated on Sepolia on Oct. 6, ahead of its now-postponed Hoodi deployment.

Coinbase Fined Again in Ireland, This Time $3.6M Over Fund Safeguarding - Decrypt
text:
Coinbase’s Irish arm has been fined roughly $3.6 million by the Central Bank of Ireland for failing to properly protect customer funds, the regulator’s second enforcement action against the exchange’s European operations in less than a year.
The regulator said Thursday it penalized Coinbase Ireland €3,252,618 for breaching safeguarding and outsourcing rules under the country’s Electronic Money Regulations between November 2020 and August 2025.
The figure reflects a 30% discount off a €4,646,597 penalty for settling, which Coinbase Ireland reached with the regulator on Oct. 21. The sanction still requires confirmation by Ireland’s High Court before taking effect.
Coinbase Ireland is an e-money institution within the broader Coinbase Group, issuing the digital money customers use to buy crypto on the platform. The Central Bank found three main failures: the company leaned too heavily on its U.S.-based parent to handle safeguarding processes required under Irish and EU rules, lacked enough local expertise to oversee the protection of customer funds, and allowed its designated safeguarding account to be underfunded for lengthy periods. It also faulted the firm’s internal controls and its failure to flag material safeguarding changes to the regulator.
Coinbase Ireland admitted the breaches. Karen O’Leary, the Central Bank’s director of enforcement, said payment and e-money firms have a “fundamental obligation to fully safeguard customers’ funds” and that the regulator has “no tolerance for weaknesses in safeguarding arrangements.”
O’Leary added that failing to honor assurances made during authorization, or to report material changes, was “completely unacceptable.”
The penalty is the second Irish hit to Coinbase’s European business this year. The Central Bank fined a separate Coinbase entity, Coinbase Europe, €21.5 million in May over anti-money-laundering failures.
Coinbase has leaned on Ireland as its EU hub, securing an e-money license there ahead of Brexit and later obtaining a MiCA license to passport its services across the bloc.
The action lands even as Coinbase expands its European footprint, having recently rolled out crypto futures for traders in the region. It also underscores how the exchange’s reliance on a single jurisdiction for EU access carries regulatory risk, with Irish authorities signaling they intend to hold firms to the commitments they made to win market entry.

title: Bitcoin Core Changes Security Policy Amid AI Risks
text:
Bitcoin Core says keeping certain vulnerabilities secret no longer offers much protection in the wake of AI-assisted bug hunting.
Bitcoin Core is changing how it handles security vulnerabilities, explaining that large language models have made certain software flaws significantly easier to discover.
In an email to the Bitcoin Development Mailing List on Thursday, Bitcoin Core developer Antoine Poinsot said that in the past, vulnerabilities were generally kept under lengthy disclosure embargoes to give users time to upgrade before details became public.
Maintaining that secrecy generally meant fixes could not be backported to older software versions, leaving users waiting until the next major release. However, Poinsot said LLMs have made some flaws so easy to rediscover that delaying fixes offers little protection.
“The embargo period achieves little but it delays the availability of a fixed release,” said Poinsot. “We are therefore updating our policy disclosure to accommodate those.”
The change comes as AI-assisted security research puts pressure on developers across Bitcoin’s software ecosystem.
Under the updated policy, vulnerabilities deemed “easily discoverable” will receive fixes as soon as possible across all maintained major versions, with security advisories published alongside the updates.
“This classification applies to vulnerabilities that can be discovered with minimal effort, such as through a simple LLM prompt,” it said.
Related: PHP flaw draws millions of exploit attempts, Cloudflare CEO warns
Other vulnerabilities will continue to follow disclosure schedules based on severity, ranging from critical flaws that threaten Bitcoin’s fundamental security to lower-risk bugs with limited impact on individual nodes.
Bitcoin Core said low-severity vulnerabilities will be disclosed two weeks after the release of a major version containing the fix, while medium and high vulnerabilities will be disclosed two weeks after the last affected release hits its “End of Life,” typically a year after the fix is released in the new major version.
“Critical bugs are not considered in the standard policy, as they would most likely require an ad-hoc procedure,” it said.
“I’ve disagreed with Antoine’s approach to security in the past, but this is a good update,” said Luke de Wolf, host of the Bitcoin Infinity Show and author of “Defending Bitcoin.”
In August, the volunteer Bitcoin Red Team reported nearly 5,000 potential issues across 390 projects, although only around a fifth of its findings had been reproduced at that point.
That month, Core Lightning developers urged operators to upgrade or take their nodes offline after receiving multiple AI-generated vulnerability reports, while withholding technical details for two weeks.

Tesla's Profit Drops 43% as Musk Starts Building Robots and Plans to Sell Driverless Cabs - Decrypt
text:
Tesla’s profit fell 43% last quarter to $787 million, down from $1.37 billion a year earlier, per its quarterly filing. The carmaker poured money into humanoid robots and driverless taxis while delivering about 2% fewer cars.
Revenue stayed flat at $28.05 billion, but operating profit, which is what’s left after the costs of running the business, fell 56% to $718 million. Research spending rose 69% to $2.76 billion, and capital expenditures, the money spent on factories and equipment, more than doubled to $4.73 billion.
That spending targets two products headed for factory floors and city streets. Optimus is a humanoid robot meant to take over dangerous and repetitive jobs, and the Cybercab is a two-seat robotaxi (a self-driving taxi you summon from an app) with no steering wheel or pedals.
Tesla said Wednesday that Optimus has entered production, and an executive said on the earnings call that the company is trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of the year.
Optimus is now coming off a production line at Tesla’s Fremont, California, factory. “The bots coming off this line are the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured,” Tesla wrote in its shareholder letter.
Musk wants to reach 20,000 Optimus units a week, but said getting there will take at least a year because the design is still changing. He put deliveries to outside customers around the end of 2027 and called the robot’s hand the hardest hardware problem, along with whether it holds up beyond a month of use.
Tesla has missed Optimus targets before, including a goal of about 10,000 robots in 2025, and rivals are already in the race. Figure AI, a startup backed by Microsoft, OpenAI and Nvidia, unveiled its Figure 02 humanoid in 2024.
On the Cybercab, Lars Moravy, Tesla’s vice president of vehicle engineering, said on the earnings call that they may be available this year: “We’re trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026.” Every Cybercab built so far is headed to Tesla’s own robotaxi fleet, and Musk said most will stay Tesla-owned and offered as “transport as a service.”
Tesla has not said who will buy Cybercabs first, though it posted a form last month for people interested in buying robotaxis, and it has not announced a price. The target price Tesla has cited is under $30,000.
Musk said the robotaxi business should become noticeable in Tesla’s overall financials in the second quarter of 2027 and will “probably” be “a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.” Tesla has not disclosed how much money the service brings in.
Musk also said Tuesday, on SpaceX’s earnings call, that the Tesla and SpaceX boards have each formed special committees of independent directors to study a combination, and no terms have been agreed.
A deal needs support from holders of 50% of all outstanding Tesla shares, a hurdle Musk called “quite a high hurdle,” and Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting is December 3, though no merger vote is on the agenda.

title: Switzerland Approves First Retail Spot Bitcoin ETF
text:
BIT Asset Management’s Bitcoin Fund ETF is expected to begin trading on SIX Swiss Exchange in November, with its public offering restricted to Switzerland.
Switzerland’s financial regulator FINMA’s first approved spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund for retail investors is expected to begin trading in November.
On Tuesday, FINMA announced it had approved the country’s first spot Bitcoin ETF that invests directly in Bitcoin, but did not disclose who the issuer was.
On Thursday, BIT Asset Management said its Bitcoin Fund ETF (BBIT) is expected to begin trading on SIX Swiss Exchange next month. The fund holds Bitcoin directly and is approved for public offering in Switzerland only.
“Most bitcoin products listed in Europe today are exchange-traded products (ETPs), which are debt instruments that carry issuer risk,” said BIT Asset Management.
The Bitcoin Fund ETF is instead a Swiss collective investment scheme, where assets are held separately from those of the fund management company and are “ring-fenced” for investors, it said.
The fund falls under Switzerland’s “other funds for alternative investments” category with particular risk. FINMA noted that other fund providers have also submitted applications for Bitcoin ETFs.
While FINMA has allowed funds that invest primarily in a basket of cryptocurrencies since 2021, this is the first time that FINMA has approved a fund that only invests in Bitcoin, citing trading history and higher trading volume compared with other cryptocurrencies.
However, it stressed that Bitcoin remains highly volatile even when accessed through an approved ETF.

title: Hegseth Bans Pentagon Insider Bets on Military Operations
text:
Hegseth warned that prediction market wagers could expose military operations to adversaries.
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has barred all Pentagon staff from using undisclosed information to place wagers on upcoming military action, including on prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket.
In a memo sent to senior Pentagon and defense agencies on Tuesday, Hegseth said all Department of War personnel are prohibited from engaging in financial transactions using nonpublic information. This involves both classified and unclassified information.
“Make no mistake why this matters. Our enemies watch movements in these markets,” Hegseth wrote. “The lives of our Service members often depend on the enemy not knowing what is coming.”
“Beyond operational security, financial stakes can warp judgment. A logistician with money riding on a strike date has an interest in that date. An analyst with a position on an outcome has an interest in that outcome,” he said.
The directive follows the April indictment of US Army soldier Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who allegedly used classified information about the operation to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro to make more than $400,000 on Polymarket.
Prosecutors allege Van Dyke participated in planning and executing the operation, then used his advance knowledge to wager on outcomes related to Maduro’s removal. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
In February, Israeli authorities arrested and indicted a military reservist and a civilian for allegedly using classified information to place bets on Polymarket related to Israeli military strikes on Iran.
